explanations.textZh:
3...NG4

黑方拯救了他们的马并攻击了 e5 兵。白方可以选择现在或稍后将棋子还给棋子，以换取空间和/或棋子的发展。白棋有可能保住棋子，但要付出位置代价。主要选项是

4. e4、4. Nf3 或 4. Bf4。

把典当还给

4. e4，阿廖欣变体让棋子立即后退，以换取在中心占据空间。 4. e4 增加了白方对 d5 的控制，并揭示了对黑方马的攻击，因此黑方的棋步几乎总是 4...Nxe5 5. f4 和黑方在 5...Nec6 或 5...Ng6 之间进行选择。黑方的一个想法是...Bb4+，希望 Nc3 Bxc3+ bxc3 给白方留下双重孤立的 c 兵。

4. Nf3，阿德勒变体，在防守兵的同时发展出一个棋子。黑棋可以迫使白棋在这条线上交还棋子，因为走棋 4...Bc5：这迫使白棋下 5。e3 结束对 f2 的压力，因此白棋不能再下 Bf4，因此无法为棋子带来足够的防守者。 （除 5. e3 之外的任何内容都是恐怖表演，例如 5. Bf4?? Bxf2+ 6. Kd2 d6 7. exd6 Qf6 8. e3 Nxe3 9. Bxe3 Qxb2+）。

5.e3后，白方可以集中精力发展，让黑方拿起棋子。延续是 5...Nc6 6. Nc3 O-O 7. Be2 Re8 8. O-O Ngxe5 9. Nxe5 Nxe5。黑方常见的中局计划是用...a5、...Ra6 和...Rh6 来拉力。

或者 4...Nc6 允许白方引入主教来保卫棋子，5. Bf4，并转置为鲁宾斯坦变体。

暂时保留选项

4. Bf4是鲁宾斯坦变体和主线延续。这里 4...Bc5？是一个错误，因为 5. e3 阻碍了 f2 并发现了对黑方马的攻击：5...d6（允许后王的主教保卫马） 6. exd6 cxd6 并且白方继续成为棋子。

然后继续是 4...Nc6 5。Nf3 Bb4+ 然后白方必须决定他们有多想保留棋子（见图）。黑方在 e5 上有两名攻击者，并且可以通过 ...Qe7 带来第三名攻击者。白棋有两名防守者，要带第三名防守者需要下Qd5：

用 6.NC3 阻止检查，保留 Qd5 的选项，但允许 6...Bxc3+ 7.bxc3，而白方的双倍、孤立的 c 兵将是一个长期的弱点。

主线是 6.Nd2，阻止检查并阻止 Qd5，因此允许黑方在 6...Qe7 后赢回棋子。

但这两种方法对于白棋来说都是可行的。一个著名的陷阱是 6. Nd2 Qe7 7. a3（攻击主教？） Ngxe5 8. axb4?? Nd3#（电子兵被黑方后固定）。

不惜一切代价保住棋子？

4. Qd5？！，防守兵而攻击黑方的马，是一个错误。 4...d6 攻击兵并让后的主教保护马，...Nc6 踢后在路上。 5. exd6（“兑现”棋子）让黑棋的主教发展 5...Bxd6，白棋必须小心不要犯错...Bb4+ 发现了对白棋后的攻击。

与 4.f4？白方决心保留棋子，但代价高昂。 4...Bc5 之后，白方必须用叉子避免 Bf2+ 或 Nf2 的威胁，很容易落后，例如5. Nh3（防守f2）O-O 6. e4（准备主教发展，发现对黑方骑士的攻击） d6（防守骑士） 7. exd6 Re8 威胁...Rxe4+ Be2 Qh4+。

explanations.pageTitle: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. c4/2...e5/3. dxe5/3...Ng4/4. Bf4
explanations.text:
This is called the "Rubinstein variation" in reference to the famous game Rubinstein – Vidmar (Berlin 1918) where the move 4.Bf4 was first employed. The move 4.Bf4 first aims to be able to answer 4...Bc5 with 5.e3 without blocking the Bc1, contrary to what happens in the Adler line 4.Nf3. On the other hand, the early development of the bishop means that White is slightly exposed to a Bb4+.

Also, in the Adler line White faces the risk of a strong attack against his kingside, while in the 4.Bf4 variation this is seldom the case because White's Bf4 is well placed to protect White's kingside if needed. However, in some cases the Bf4 can become slightly exposed (e.g. some variations of the Rubinstein line when Black plays g7–g5 and h7–h5).

Apart from the sideline 4...g5, the main line continues with both camps developing their pieces around the e5-pawn with 4...Nc6 5.Nf3 Bb4+ (preparing 6...Qe7) when White has an important choice to make between the two moves 6.Nc3 and 6.Nbd2, each leading to extremely different play. With 6.Nc3 White accepts to have his pawn structure on the queenside ruined, in return for a material advantage of one pawn, the bishop pair and active play in the center.

On the other hand, with 6.Nbd2 White gives back the gambited pawn in order to keep a healthy pawn structure and to get the bishop pair. After 6...Qe7 White generally plays 7.a3 in order to force the immediate exchange of the Bb4 for the Nd2 and get the bishop pair, a space advantage and a minority attack on the queenside. White can also try 7.e3 which tries to win a tempo over the 7.a3 variation but may end up with the Bb4/Nd2 exchange made in less favorable circumstances, or not made at all. The maverick gambit 6...f6 or 6...d6 also exist.

explanations.textZh:
这被称为“鲁宾斯坦变体”，源自著名的鲁宾斯坦-维德玛游戏（柏林，1918 年），其中首次采用了 4.Bf4 着法。移动 4.Bf4 首先旨在能够用 5.e3 回答 4...Bc5，而不阻塞 Bc1，这与 Adler 行 4.Nf3 中发生的情况相反。另一方面，象的早期发展意味着白棋稍微暴露于 Bb4+。

此外，在阿德勒路线中，白方面临着对其王翼进行强力攻击的风险，而在 4.Bf4 变体中，这种情况很少发生，因为白方的 Bf4 处于有利位置，可以在需要时保护白方的王翼。然而，在某些情况下，Bf4 可能会稍微暴露（例如，当黑棋下 g7-g5 和 h7-h5 时鲁宾斯坦线的一些变化）。

除了边线 4...g5 之外，主线继续，两个阵营都围绕着 4...Nc6 5.Nf3 Bb4+（准备 6...Qe7）的 e5 棋子开发自己的棋子，此时白方在 6.Nc3 和 6.Nbd2 两步棋之间做出重要选择，每步棋都会导致极其不同的玩法。 6.Nc3 白方接受毁掉他在后侧的棋子结构，以换取一个棋子、主教对和中心的积极发挥的物质优势。

另一方面，白方用 6.Nbd2 返还已下棋的棋子，以保持健康的棋子结构并获得象对。 6后...Qe7白方通常会下7.a3，以迫使Bb4立即交换Nd2并获得主教对，空间优势和后翼的少数进攻。白棋也可以尝试 7.e3，它试图赢得比 7.a3 变体更快的节奏，但最终可能会在不太有利的情况下进行 Bb4/Nd2 交换，或者根本不进行。特立独行的策略 6...f6 或 6...d6 也存在。

explanations.pageTitle: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. c4/2...e5/3. dxe5/3...Ng4/4. Bf4/4...Nc6/5. Nf3/5...Bb4/6. Nc3
explanations.text:
This line is called the "Kornl Richter gambit" by the chess historian Bill Wall.; this is the only line of the Budapest gambit in which Black cannot regain his pawn for sure. Black does best to immediately exchange the Nc3 with 6...Bxc3+ 7.bxc3 as otherwise White gets a small positional advantage simply by avoiding the doubled pawns. Then Black can put pressure on the e5-pawn with 7...Qe7 when White's only possibility to keep the pawn is 8.Qd5. At this stage, White's position has several defects notably:

two pairs of doubled pawns (in c3&c4, and in e2&e5),

a king in the centre who still needs two tempi before being able to castle,

a queen in the centre as well, who will be subject to attacks by black minor pieces.

White also has long-term trumps, however, and notably he is still a pawn up (the e5-pawn) and he has the bishop pair. Moreover, White currently threatens to ease the pressure with the move 9.h3 that would put the Ng4 on the unfavourable square h6, so Black must keep the initiative with active moves like 8...Qa3 (attacking the c3-pawn) or 8...f6 (attacking the e5-pawn once more).

Line 8...Qa3

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Bf4 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bb4+ 6.Nc3 Bxc3+ 7.bxc3 Qe7 8.Qd5 Qa3

The line 8...Qa3 puts pressure on the white queenside pawns, this pressure can latter be reinforced with the manoeuvre Nf6–e4. The black queen can also access to the a5-square at some point, where it puts pressure on the e1–a5 diagonal towards the white king.

An interesting sideline is 9.Rd1!? aiming to open the position and seize the initiative even at the cost of the doubled pawns. For instance, after 9...Qxc3+ 10.Qd2!? Qxc4 11. h3 Nh6 12.e3 Qb4 13.Qxb4 Nxb4 14.a3 Nc6 15.Bc4 White has good compensation for the pawn thanks to its bishop pair and good development. Another fringe possibility is 9.Qd3, after which Mieses continued by 9...Qa5 in his game against Rubinstein. The game followed up with 10.Rc1 Ngxe5 11.Nxe5 Nxe5 12.Qg3 with a double attack against the pawns in c7 and g7. White will be a pawn up but his queenside pawn are weak and he is slightly behind in development.

The most common move, however, is 9.Rc1 playing on the fact that 9...Qxa2?! 10.h3 Nh6 11.e4 Qa3 12.Be2 gives White a clear advantage with the bishop pair and the black Nh6 awkwardly placed. So Black prefers 9...f6 10.exf6 Nxf6 and White has to choose between three possible queen retreats:

The simplest is 11.Qd1!? d6 12.Qb3 and White has a slight advantage. He retains the extra pawn, and the black queen would be better of on the e7-square than on the a3-square.

Strangely enough, 11.Qd2 is the most frequently played although it is not the best: Lalic thinks 11.Qd2 is inappropriate and gives Black excellent counterplay, while Moskalenko considers that the white queen is passive on the d2-square. After 11.Qd2 d6 12.Nd4 0-0 we reach the position of a famous game between Rubinstein and Vidmar, the first tournament game between grandmasters with the Budapest gambit. Rubinstein erred with 13.e3? when the Bf4 is cut from the queenside, so that Black can show the weakness of White's dark squares with 13...Nxd4! 14.bxc3 Ne4 15.Qc2 Qa5+ 16.Ke2 Rxf4+!. The better 13.f3 occurred in a game between O'Kelly and Heidenfeld. The correct method for Black is to target the c4-pawn with the regrouping Ne5/Qc5. After 13...Ne5 14.e4 Qc5 15.Nb3 Qc6 16.Bxe5!? dxe5 17.Qg5 Re8 18.Be2 and here Moskalenko proposes either 18...a5 to attack the queenside at once and capture the a2-pawn, either 18...b6 to block the c4-pawn and attack it later.

After 11.Qd3 0-0 12.g3 d6 13.Bg2 Black should switch to a materialistic mode with 13...Qxa2.

Line 8...f6

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Bf4 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bb4+ 6.Nc3 Bxc3+ 7.bxc3 Qe7 8.Qd5 f6

In the line 8...f6 Black concentrates on an active piece play in the centre. After 9.exf6 Nxf6 all three queen retreats 10.Qd1, 10.Qd2 and 10.Qd3 are possible but each of them has its own drawbacks: on d1 the queen is not developed, on d3 it is exposed to the manoeuvre Bc8–f5 and on d2 it is exposed to the manoeuvre Nf6–e4. Lalic considers 10.Qd3 to be the main move (as Moskalenko also does), qualifies 10.Qd1 as a "respectable option", but considers 10.Qd2 as "inaccurate", giving the line 10...d6 11.e3 Ne4 12.Qc2 g5 13.Bg3 Bf5 14.Bd3 h5 with the initiative for Black. Meanwhile Black will try to create counterplay by attacking either the weak c4-pawn, or more seldom the kingside with the pawn thrusts g7–g5 and h7–h5. In both cases a key possibility is the move Nf6–e4 that centralises the black knight, attacks the weak c3-pawn, controls the c5-square and supports the g7–g5 pawn advance.

Line 8...f6 followed by 11.e3

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Bf4 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bb4+ 6.Nc3 Bxc3+ 7.bxc3 Qe7 8.Qd5 f6 9.exf6 Nxf6 10.Qd3 d6 11.e3

Meanwhile Black will try to create counterplay by attacking either the weak c4-pawn, or more seldom the kingside with the pawn thrusts g7–g5 and h7–h5.

explanations.textZh:
这条路线被国际象棋历史学家比尔·沃尔称为“科恩·里克特策略”。这是布达佩斯策略中黑方无法肯定夺回棋子的唯一路线。黑方最好立即用 6...Bxc3+ 7.bxc3 交​​换 Nc3，否则白方只需避开双兵即可获得较小的位置优势。然后黑方可以用 7...Qe7 对 e5 兵施加压力，而白方保留该兵的唯一可能性是 8.Qd5。现阶段，白方的立场有几个明显的缺陷：

两对双棋子（在 c3&c4 中，以及在 e2&e5 中），

位于中心的国王仍需要两个节奏才能攻城略地，

中间还有一个皇后，她会受到黑色小棋子的攻击。

然而，怀特也有长期王牌，值得注意的是他仍然是一个棋子（e5-棋子）并且他有主教对。此外，白方目前威胁要通过 9.h3 棋来缓解压力，这会将 Ng4 置于不利的方格 h6 上，因此黑棋必须通过 8...Qa3（攻击 c3 棋子）或 8...f6（再次攻击 e5 棋子）等主动棋来保持主动。

8号线...Qa3

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Bf4 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bb4+ 6.Nc3 Bxc3+ 7.bxc3 Qe7 8.Qd5 Qa3

线 8...Qa3 对白色后侧棋子施加压力，这种压力可以通过 Nf6-e4 机动来加强。黑后也可以在某个时刻进入 a5 方格，从而对 e1-a5 对角线向白王施加压力。

一个有趣的副线是 9.Rd1!?旨在即使不惜双倍棋子的代价，也能开仓并掌握主动。例如，在 9...Qxc3+ 10.Qd2! 之后Qxc4 11. h3 Nh6 12.e3 Qb4 13.Qxb4 Nxb4 14.a3 Nc6 15.Bc4 由于其主教对和良好的发展，白方对棋子有良好的补偿。另一个边缘可能性是 9.Qd3，之后米塞斯在与鲁宾斯坦的比赛中继续了 9...Qa5。比赛随后以 10.Rc1 Ngxe5 11.Nxe5 Nxe5 12.Qg3 对 c7 和 g7 中的棋子进行双重攻击。白棋将是一个棋子，但他的后侧棋子很弱，而且他的发展稍稍落后。

然而，最常见的着法是 9.Rc1，因为 9...Qxa2？！ 10.h3 Nh6 11.e4 Qa3 12.Be2 为白方提供了明显的优势，而黑方 Nh6 则处于尴尬的位置。因此黑方更喜欢 9...f6 10.exf6 Nxf6，而白方必须在三种可能的后撤退之间进行选择：

最简单的是11.Qd1！？ d6 12.Qb3 和白棋稍占优势。他保留了多余的棋子，而黑皇后在 e7 方格上比在 a3 方格上更好。

奇怪的是，11.Qd2 虽然不是最好的，但却是最常使用的：Lalic 认为 11.Qd2 不合适，并为黑方提供了极好的反击，而 Moskalenko 则认为白后在 d2 方格上处于被动。 11.Qd2 d6 12.Nd4 0-0 之后，我们进入了鲁宾斯坦和维德玛之间一场著名比赛的位置，这是大师之间采用布达佩斯策略的第一场锦标赛比赛。鲁宾斯坦在 13.e3 上犯了错误？当Bf4从后侧切掉时，黑方可以用13...Nxd4来显示白方暗方的弱点！ 14.bxc3 Ne4 15.Qc2 Qa5+ 16.Ke2 Rxf4+！。更好的13.f3发生在奥凯利和海登菲尔德之间的一场比赛中。黑棋的正确方法是用重新组合的 Ne5/Qc5 来瞄准 c4 兵。 13之后...Ne5 14.e4 Qc5 15.Nb3 Qc6 16.Bxe5！？ dxe5 17.Qg5 Re8 18.Be2 在这里，Moskalenko 建议使用 18...a5 立即攻击后翼并捕获 a2-pawn，或者使用 18...b6 阻挡 c4-pawn 并稍后攻击它。

11.Qd3 0-0 12.g3 d6 13.Bg2 黑方应切换至唯物模式 13...Qxa2。

8号线...f6

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Bf4 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bb4+ 6.Nc3 Bxc3+ 7.bxc3 Qe7 8.Qd5 f6

在 8...f6 线上，黑方专注于中间的活跃棋子。 9.exf6 Nxf6 之后，所有三个后撤退 10.Qd1、10.Qd2 和 10.Qd3 都是可能的，但它们各自都有其自己的缺点：在 d1 上，皇后未发育，在 d3 上，它暴露于机动 Bc8–f5，在 d2 上，它暴露于机动 Nf6–e4。 Lalic 认为 10.Qd3 是主要棋步（Moskalenko 也是如此），将 10.Qd1 视为“值得尊敬的选择”，但认为 10.Qd2 是“不准确的”，给出了 10...d6 11.e3 Ne4 12.Qc2 g5 13.Bg3 Bf5 14.Bd3 h5 行，黑棋先动。与此同时，黑方将尝试通过攻击较弱的 c4 兵，或更罕见地使用兵推力 g7-g5 和 h7-h5 攻击王侧来创造反击。在这两种情况下，一个关键的可能性是走Nf6-e4，它集中黑马，攻击弱的c3兵，控制c5方并支持g7-g5兵前进。

第 8...f6 行，后跟 11.e3

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Bf4 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bb4+ 6.Nc3 Bxc3+ 7.bxc3 Qe7 8.Qd5 f6 9.exf6 Nxf6 10.Qd3 d6 11.e3

与此同时，黑方将尝试通过攻击较弱的 c4 兵，或更罕见地使用兵推力 g7-g5 和 h7-h5 攻击王侧来创造反击。

explanations.pageTitle: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. c4/2...e5/3. dxe5/3...Ng4/4. Bf4/4...Nc6/5. Nf3/5...Bb4/6. Nbd2
explanations.text:
With 6.Nbd2 White gives back the gambited pawn in order to keep a healthy pawn structure and to get the bishop pair. After 6...Qe7 White has two important possibilities:

7.a3 to force the immediate exchange of the Bb4 for the Nd2 and get the bishop pair, a space advantage and a minority attack on the queenside.

7.e3 to win a tempo over the 7.a3 variation but it may end up with the Bb4/Nd2 exchange made in less favorable circumstances, or not made at all.

The maverick gambit 6...f6 also exists.

The line 6.Nbd2 Qe7 7.a3

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Bf4 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bb4+ 6.Nbd2 Qe7 7.a3

The Bb4 is attacked but Black does not have to move it for the moment, and instead plays 7...Ngxe5 to get the gambitted pawn back. Now Black threatens both to take the c4 pawn and to take the Nf3, when White will either have to accept doubled pawns or move his king. For example this is seen after 8.e3?! when 8...Nxf3+ forces either 9.gxf3 or 9.Qxf3 Bxd2+ 10.Kxd2, when White cannot castle anymore.

White cannot play 8.axb4?? because of the Kieninger trap 8...Nd3 mate. White does not want to play 8.Bxe5?! either because it would lose the bishop pair, which is the main source of White's hopes for an advantage in the Bernstein line. So White is more or less forced to exchange a pair of knights with 8.Nxe5 Nxe5.

White still cannot win a piece with 9.axb4?? because the mate threat by Nd3# is still in force. White also cannot win a piece by 9.Bxe5?! because Black would play the zwischenzug 9...Bxd2+ 10.Qxd2 Qxe5 with an equal game. White accordingly plays 9.e3 in order to protect the c4-pawn that was attacked by the Ne5.

Now there is no more mating threat on d3 so the Bb4 is really attacked and Black has to move it. 9...Bd6 (or 9...Bc5 10.b4 Bd6, intending to meet 11.c5?! with 11...Nd3+ 12.Bxd3 Bxf4) would misplace the bishop, and 9...Ba5?? would lose the bishop to 10.b4 Bb6 11.c5. That leaves 9...Bxd2+, when after 10.Qxd2 we get the real starting position of this variation.

It is important to note that for Black, the sequence 7...Ngxe5 8...Nxe5 9...Bxd2+ is not only cunning, but also the best move-order as another sequence would give White an early opportunity to realise the advantageous c4–c5 push. For example after 7...Bxd2+?! 8.Qxd2 Ngxe5 9.Nxe5 Nxe5 White should not play the usual 10.e3?! but should strive for more with the immediate 10.c5! as Black cannot take in c5 without losing the c7-pawn (because of the possibilities Ra1–c1 and Qd2–c3).

After 10.Qxd2, Tseitlin explains that "opening manuals assess this position as favourable to White on the basis of the bishop pair. However, considering the closed nature of the position, White faces substantial difficulties in the realisation of this nominal advantage." Black has not a lot of things to be proud of as there are no targets in White's camp, but can put up a lot of resistance thanks to some small assets:

Black's Ne5 is strongly centralized, attacks the c4-pawn, and restricts the Bf1 from moving to the natural squares d3 and f3. Moreover, exchanging the knight with Bxe5 is not appealing for White, since that would mean losing the advantage of the bishop pair.

the Bc8 can sometimes become better than its counterpart the Bf1, if it makes it to the good squares b7 or c6 while the Bf1 remains restricted by the Ne5.

This explains the most natural plans for both sides. White will try a minority attack on the queenside, in order to increase its space advantage and to create some weaknesses in the black pawns (e.g. an isolated pawn or a backward pawn). So White will try to use the advances b2–b4 or c4–c5 in good conditions, supported by the queen and the rooks on the c-file and the d-file. On the other hand, Black will try to keep the position closed, most importantly keep the c4-pawn where it is in order to keep the Bf1 at bay. This can be achieved by moves like b7–b6 and d7–d6, and sometimes the manoeuvre Ne5–d7–f8–e6.

The first move by Black has to be 10...d6! because otherwise White plays 11.c5! and gets a clear advantage immediately. For example 10...b6? loses a pawn to 11.Qd5 Nc6 (forced) 12.Bxc7, and 10...O-O?! is bad because of 11.c5! when Black should not take with 11...Qxc5? because of 12.Rc1 Qe7 13.Rxc7 and White is winning already.

The line 6.Nbd2 Qe7 7.e3

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Bf4 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bb4+ 6.Nbd2 Qe7 7.e3

In this variation White tries to avoid the move a2–a3 in order to gain a tempo over the 7.a3 variation. After the standard moves 7...Ngxe5 8.Nxe5 Nxe5 9.Be2 Black has the main line 9...0-0 or the less-explored 9...b6. While 9...0-0 will give him the option on the tenth move to keep his Bb4 bishop or part with it, 9...b6 is more forcing as Black will be more or less compelled to exchange his bishop for the Nd2.

Lalic thinks the strategies in which Black gives up the bishop pair (by exchanging its Bb4 for the Nd2) for nothing are a mistake. He does not like the strategy to retreat the Bb4 in d6 either, because they are too drawish.

explanations.textZh:
6.Nbd2 白方归还已下棋的棋子，以保持健康的棋子结构并获得象对。 6...Qe7 白棋之后有两种重要的可能性：

7.a3迫使Bb4立即交换Nd2并获得主教对，空间优势和后翼的少数进攻。

7.e3 比 7.a3 变体赢得了节奏，但最终可能会在不太有利的情况下进行 Bb4/Nd2 交换，或者根本不进行交换。

特立独行的策略 6...f6 也存在。

6.Nbd2 Qe7 7.a3 行

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Bf4 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bb4+ 6.Nbd2 Qe7 7.a3

Bb4 受到攻击，但黑方暂时不必移动它，而是下 7...Ngxe5 以收回已出局的棋子。现在，黑方威胁既要拿下 c4 兵，又要拿下 Nf3，而白方要么必须接受双兵，要么移动他的王。例如，这是在 8.e3 之后看到的？！当 8...Nxf3+ 强制 9.gxf3 或 9.Qxf3 Bxd2+ 10.Kxd2 时，当白方无法再城堡时。

白棋不能下8.axb4？？因为基宁格陷阱 8...Nd3 伴侣。白棋不想玩8.Bxe5？！要么是因为它会失去主教对，这是怀特希望在伯恩斯坦线中获得优势的主要来源。所以白棋或多或少被迫与8.Nxe5 Nxe5交换一对马。

白棋9.axb4仍然无法获胜？因为 Nd3# 的伴侣威胁仍然有效。白棋也不能以9.Bxe5获胜？！因为黑棋会以同等的比分下 zwischenzug 9...Bxd2+ 10.Qxd2 Qxe5。白方因此下9.e3以保护被Ne5攻击的c4兵。

现在 d3 上不再有交配威胁，因此 Bb4 确实受到攻击，黑方必须移动它。 9...Bd6（或 9...Bc5 10.b4 Bd6，打算与 11.c5 相遇？！用 11...Nd3+ 12.Bxd3 Bxf4）会迷失主教，而 9...Ba5??将失去主教 10.b4 Bb6 11.c5。剩下 9...Bxd2+，当 10.Qxd2 之后我们得到这个变化的真正起始位置。

值得注意的是，对于黑方来说，序列 7...Ngxe5 8...Nxe5 9...Bxd2+ 不仅是狡猾的，而且也是最好的走法，因为另一个序列将给白方一个早期的机会来实现有利的 c4-c5 推进。例如 7...Bxd2+ 之后？！ 8.Qxd2 Ngxe5 9.Nxe5 Nxe5 白棋不应该玩通常的10.e3？！但应该争取更多的即时 10.c5！因为黑方无法在不失去 c7 兵的情况下接受 c5（因为存在 Ra1–c1 和 Qd2–c3 的可能性）。

在 10.Qxd2 之后，Tseitlin 解释说，“开局手册根据象对评估这一局面对白方有利。然而，考虑到该局面的封闭性，白方在实现这一名义优势方面面临着巨大的困难。”黑方没有太多值得骄傲的事情，因为白方阵营中没有目标，但由于一些小资产，黑方可以提出很大的阻力：

黑方的 Ne5 是强中心化的，攻击 c4 兵，并限制 Bf1 移动到自然格 d3 和 f3。此外，用 Bxe5 交换马对白方来说没有吸引力，因为这意味着失去象对的优势。

如果 Bc8 进入好的方格 b7 或 c6，而 Bf1 仍然受到 Ne5 的限制，则 Bc8 有时会变得比其对应的 Bf1 更好。

这解释了双方最自然的计划。白方将尝试对后侧进行少数攻击，以增加其空间优势并在黑棋中制造一些弱点（例如孤立的棋子或落后的棋子）。因此，白棋会在良好的条件下尝试使用b2-b4或c4-c5的进步，并得到c线和d线的后和车的支持。另一方面，黑方将尝试保持局面封闭，最重要的是让 c4 兵保持在原位，以阻止 Bf1。这可以通过 b7-b6 和 d7-d6 等动作来实现，有时还可以通过 Ne5-d7-f8-e6 动作来实现。

黑棋的第一步必须是 10...d6！因为否则白方下 11.c5！并立即获得明显优势。例如10...b6？失去一个棋子给 11.Qd5 Nc6（强制）12.Bxc7 和 10...O-O？！因为 11.c5 很糟糕！黑棋什么时候不应该下 11...Qxc5？因为 12.Rc1 Qe7 13.Rxc7 并且白棋已经获胜。

6.Nbd2 Qe7 7.e3 行

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Bf4 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bb4+ 6.Nbd2 Qe7 7.e3

在这个变体中，白方试图避免走a2-a3，以获得超过7.a3变体的节奏。标准走法 7...Ngxe5 8.Nxe5 Nxe5 9.Be2 黑方有主线 9...0-0 或较少探索的 9...b6。虽然 9...0-0 将让他在第十步棋时可以选择保留 Bb4 象或放弃它，但 9...b6 更具强迫性，因为黑方将或多或少被迫用 Nd2 交换他的象。

Lalic 认为黑方白白放弃象对（通过将 Bb4 换成 Nd2）的策略是错误的。他也不喜欢d6中撤退Bb4的策略，因为它们太吸引人了。

explanations.text:
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Bf4 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bb4+ 6.Nbd2 Qe7 7.a3 Ngxe5 8.Nxe5 Nxe5 9.e3 Bxd2+ 10.Qxd2 d6

After 10...d6! White can try (and has tried) about any move that goes into the direction of the aforementioned plan. In particular White has to chose if he wants to start active operations on the queenside immediately (e.g. Rc1, Qc3, c5), or if he wants to finish his development first (with Be2 and 0-0).

The immediate 11.c5!? is a possible pawn sacrifice in order to open some diagonals for the bishops. As Lalic points out, "after 11...dxc5 Black's knight on e5 has lost its support and therefore all tactical motifs based on Qd5 and Bb5+ must be carefully checked". White gets a powerful attack for his pawn but nothing decisive, for example 11...dxc5 12.Qd5 Nc6! 13.Bb5 0-0 14.Bxc6 bxc6 15.Qxc6 Rb8 with a fully viable game according to an analysis from Tseitlin. Another retreat for the knight also occurred, with 11...dxc5 12.Qd5 Ng6 13.Bb5+ Bd7 14.Qxb7 0-0 15.Bxd7 Nxf4.

The same idea can be tried with the preparatory 11.Rc1, and after 11...0-0 12.c5!? dxc5 13.Qd5 Ng6 14.Bg3 White should be reminded that he has not finished his development with 14...Qf6! and a counterattack on b2. Playing Black, Svidler chose a different path with 11...b6 but his opponent Lesiège nevertheless sacrified the pawn with 12.c5!, when play continued 12...bxc5 13.b4 0-0 14.bxc5 Bb7 15.f3 and Svilder destroyed his own pawn structure with 15...dxc5!? in order to activate his pieces and make use of the d-file.

The most popular is 11.Be2 as White delays his queenside play until he has achieved castling. It also gives Black more time to organise defence on the queenside, e.g. 11...0-0 12.0-0 b6! 13.Rac1 Bb7 14.Rfd1 a5 15.b4 Nd7 and the game is still balanced.

In a game Browne tried 11.Be2 b6 12.e4 but it did not bring the expected activity and he lost.

Koepcke tried 11.Be2 0-0 12.O-O b6 13.b4 Rd8!? 14.Qc3 and then his opponent Yermolinsky uncorked the cold-blooded 14...c5!, a surprising move that creates the disadvantage of a backward pawn in d6, but Lalic considers "Black's activity is sufficient to compensate for the weakness on d6 and in fact it is the white c4-pawn that could prove vulnerable one day."

Black can also let his opponent realise the push c4–c5 with 11.Be2 0-0 12.0-0 b6 13.b4 Bb7 14.c5 and then seek counter-chances based on the possession of the d-file with 14...dxc5 15.bxc5 Rfd8.

Black can insert the preventive a7–a5 for the minor reason of delaying White's push b2–b4 and for the major reason of opening the a-file with a5xb4 once the push b2–b4 has been realised. The advantage for Black of opening the a-file is that white rooks cannot in the same time attack along the c-file and contest the a-file to the black rooks. So generally White abandons the a-file to concentrate on the attack along the c-file, and Black can use the a-file for its own purposes. For example a game Lavrov – Kaposztas saw the moves 11.Be2 0-0 12.0-0 a5 13.Rac1 b6 14.Bg3 Bg7 15.Qc3 Rfe8 16.Rfd1 Nd7 17.b4 axb4 18.axb4 Nf6, with a double-edged position.

After 10...d6! White can try (and has tried) about any move that goes into the direction of the aforementioned plan. Notes
explanations.textZh:
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Bf4 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bb4+ 6.Nbd2 Qe7 7.a3 Ngxe5 8.Nxe5 Nxe5 9.e3 Bxd2+ 10.Qxd2 d6

10...d6 后！白棋可以尝试（并且已经尝试过）任何朝着上述计划方向发展的举动。特别是，白方必须选择是否要立即在后翼开始积极行动（例如 Rc1、Qc3、c5），或者是否要首先完成他的发展（Be2 和 0-0）。

立即的11.c5！？是一个可能的典当牺牲，以便为主教打开一些对角线。正如 Lalic 指出的，“11...dxc5 之后，e5 上的黑方骑士失去了支持，因此必须仔细检查所有基于 Qd5 和 Bb5+ 的战术主题”。白方的棋子获得了强大的攻击，但没有什么决定性的，例如 11...dxc5 12.Qd5 Nc6！ 13.Bb5 0-0 14.Bxc6 bxc6 15.Qxc6 Rb8 根据 Tseitlin 的分析，这是一场完全可行的比赛。马的另一次撤退也发生了，11...dxc5 12.Qd5 Ng6 13.Bb5+ Bd7 14.Qxb7 0-0 15.Bxd7 Nxf4。

同样的想法可以尝试用预备 11.Rc1，以及 11...0-0 12.c5 之后！？ dxc5 13.Qd5 Ng6 14.Bg3 白棋应该提醒他，他还没有完成 14...Qf6 的发展！以及对b2的反击。玩黑棋时，Svilder 选择了不同的路径 11...b6，但他的对手 Lesiège 还是用 12.c5! 牺牲了棋子，当比赛继续进行时 12...bxc5 13.b4 0-0 14.bxc5 Bb7 15.f3 而 Svilder 用 15...dxc5! 摧毁了自己的棋子结构。为了激活他的棋子并利用d文件。

最受欢迎的是 11.Be2，因为白棋推迟了他的后翼进攻，直到他实现易位。这也给了黑方更多的时间在后翼组织防守，例如： 11...0-0 12.0-0 b6！ 13.Rac1 Bb7 14.Rfd1 a5 15.b4 Nd7 比赛仍然平衡。

在一场比赛中，布朗尝试了 11.Be2 b6 12.e4，但没有带来预期的活性，他输了。

科普克尝试了 11.Be2 0-0 12.O-O b6 13.b4 Rd8！？ 14.Qc3，然后他的对手叶莫林斯基（Yermolinsky）打开了冷血的 14...c5！，这是一个令人惊讶的举动，造成了 d6 中落后棋子的劣势，但 Lalic 认为“黑方的活动足以弥补 d6 上的弱点，事实上，白棋 c4 棋子有一天可能会变得脆弱。”

黑棋还可以让对手通过 11.Be2 0-0 12.0-0 b6 13.b4 Bb7 14.c5 实现推 c4–c5，然后根据 14...dxc5 15.bxc5 Rfd8 的 d 线占有情况寻求反击机会。

黑棋可以插入预防性的a7-a5，次要原因是延迟白棋的推b2-b4，而主要原因是一旦实现了推b2-b4，就可以用a5xb4打开a文件。黑车开a字形的好处是，白车不能同时沿着c字形攻击，并与黑车争夺a字形。所以一般白方会放弃a线，集中精力沿着c线进攻，而黑方则可以利用a线来达到自己的目的。例如，拉夫罗夫 – 卡波什塔斯的棋局是 11.Be2 0-0 12.0-0 a5 13.Rac1 b6 14.Bg3 Bg7 15.Qc3 Rfe8 16.Rfd1 Nd7 17.b4 axb4 18.axb4 Nf6，具有双刃的位置。

笔记

explanations.text:
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Bf4 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bb4+ 6.Nbd2 Qe7 7.e3 Ngxe5 8.Nxe5 Nxe5 9.Be2

In this variation White tries to avoid the move a2–a3 in order to gain a tempo over the 7.a3 variation. After the standard moves 7...Ngxe5 8.Nxe5 Nxe5 9.Be2 Black has the main line 9...0-0 or the less-explored 9...b6. While 9...0-0 will give him the option on the tenth move to keep his Bb4 bishop or part with it, 9...b6 is more forcing as Black will be more or less compelled to exchange his bishop for the Nd2.

Lalic thinks the strategies in which Black gives up the bishop pair (by exchanging its Bb4 for the Nd2) for nothing are a mistake. He does not like the strategy to retreat the Bb4 in d6 either, because they are too drawish. He recommends the strategy to retreat the bishop in c5, and keep it there thanks to the push a7–a5.

Black gives up the bishop pair with 9...b6

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Bf4 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bb4+ 6.Nbd2 Qe7 7.e3 Ngxe5 8.Nxe5 Nxe5 9.Be2 b6

With 9...b6 Black intends to compensate the loss of the bishop pair (once he has exchanged his Bb4 for the Nd2) by the activity of his other bishop on the long diagonal, reasoning that White will have difficulties to do the same as his Be2 cannot go on the f3-square without being exchanged against the Ne5. The drawback of 9...b6, however, is that the b6-square is not available for the Bb4 anymore, so that this bishop will soon lack retreat squares.

Indeed, after 10.0-0 it would be dangerous to keep his Bb4 because White could start an attack aiming at harassing the black bishop. For instance in the game Etchegaray - Sebban after 10...Bb7?! 11.Nb1 a5 12.a3 Bc5 13.Nc3 Black committed suicide with the natural 13...d6??, and after the tactical sequence 14.b4! axb4 15.axb4 Rxa1 16.Qxa1 Bxb4 17.Qa4+ Nc6 18.Nd5 White wins a piece. Another example is the direct 10...Bb7?! 11.Nf3!? and unfortunately Black cannot take with his knight as after 12...Nxf3 13.Bxf3 Bxf3 14.Qxf3 both his Ra8 and his c7-pawn would be attacked.

Therefore, Black has to exchange his Bb4 for the Nd2. After 10...Bxd2 11.Qxd2 Bb7 White has indeed gained a tempo as he provoked the exchange of the Bb4 against the Nd2 without having to play a2-a3. This tempo gained will allow him to realize the push c4-c5 before Black has setup his defenses to avoid it. White can prepare the push c4–c5 with the b2–b4, with Qc3 and/or with Rac1, for instance:

In the game Solozhenkin – Stiazhkin (Leningrad 1990), White tried the immediate sacrifice 12.c5!? bxc5 13.Qa5 and after 13...d6 14.Bxe5! dxe5 15.Rfc1 White stands much better. However Black improved on these moves in the game Flear – Blatny (Andorra 1993) by giving immediately the pawn back with 13...Ng6! 14.Qxc7 Nxf4 15.Qxf4 0-0 and Lalic thinks the situation is balanced.

After 12.Qc3 the natural 12...d6!? leads after 13.c5 bxc5 14.Bxe5 Qxe5 15.Qxe5+ dxe5 16.Rac1 0-0-0 17.Rxc5 to a superior ending for White, although Lalic thinks Black should hold. Therefore another possibility for Black is trying to do without the move d7-d6, as in the game Gausel – Reite (Norwegian Team Championship, 1991) with 12.Qc3 f6 13.b4 c5!? which is a radical way to remove the c4-c5 threat.

In the game Alterman – Blatny (Pardubice 1993), White took his time to prepare the c4–c5 push, with 12.Rac1 d6 13.b4 0-0 14.c5 dxc5 15.bxc5 Rad8 16.Qc3 Ng6 17.Bg3 Rd5 18.cxb6 cxb6 19.Rfd1 Rfd8 20.Rxd5 Rxd5 21.a3 and White has succeeded in freeing his bishop pair, so he has an edge. Therefore the same Black player tried to improve his play in the game Chernin – Blatny (Brno 1993) with the immediate retreat 13...Ng6 but after 14.Bg3 0-0?! 15.c5 dxc5 16.bxc5 Rfd8 17.Qb4 White also had the initiative. Instead, Chernin suggests a wholly different plan with 14...h5!?, intending to force the exchange of the Bg3 against the Ng6, develop the Rh8 through the h6-square and put the King on f8 instead of castling.

Black gives up the bishop pair with 9...0-0

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Bf4 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bb4+ 6.Nbd2 Qe7 7.e3 Ngxe5 8.Nxe5 Nxe5 9.Be2 0-0

When Black goes for it with 10...Bxd2, he runs the risk to end up a tempo down over the 7.a3 variation and to be soon unable to meet White's positional threats on the queenside. White can avoid the push a2–a3 and continue with the standard plans of the 7.a3 variation. Tseitlin considers the main variation is 9.Be2 d6 10.0-0 Bxd2 11.Qxd2 0-0 12.Rfd1 b6 13.b4 Bb7 14.c5 dxc5 15.bxc5 and then gives a line he analysed in which Black ends a pawn down but in a drawish position. Similarly, after the moves 9.Be2 Bxd2+ 10.Qxd2 d6 11.0-0 0-0 Lalic notices: "by exchanging so early on d2 and castling quickly Black has saved himself the worry of how to meet Nb3 and what to do with his king, but such simplistic logic is in no way going to guarantee him a comfortable game."

However, everything is not that bad for Black. First, to implement his plan White has to concentrate on development (9.Be2, 10.0-0) before he turns his attention to the queenside.

explanations.textZh:
1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Bf4 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bb4+ 6.Nbd2 Qe7 7.e3 Ngxe5 8.Nxe5 Nxe5 9.Be2

在这个变体中，白方试图避免走a2-a3，以获得超过7.a3变体的节奏。标准走法 7...Ngxe5 8.Nxe5 Nxe5 9.Be2 黑方有主线 9...0-0 或较少探索的 9...b6。虽然 9...0-0 将让他在第十步棋时可以选择保留 Bb4 象或放弃它，但 9...b6 更具强迫性，因为黑方将或多或少被迫用 Nd2 交换他的象。

Lalic 认为黑方白白放弃象对（通过将 Bb4 换成 Nd2）的策略是错误的。他也不喜欢d6中撤退Bb4的策略，因为它们太吸引人了。他推荐的策略是在c5撤退主教，并通过a7-a5的推动将其保留在那里。

黑棋放弃了象对 9...b6

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Bf4 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bb4+ 6.Nbd2 Qe7 7.e3 Ngxe5 8.Nxe5 Nxe5 9.Be2 b6

9...b6 黑方打算通过长对角线上另一个象的活动来补偿象对的损失（一旦他将 Bb4 换成 Nd2），理由是白方将很难做同样的事情，因为他的 Be2 不能在不与 Ne5 交换的情况下进入 f3 方格。然而，9...b6 的缺点是 b6 方格不再适用于 Bb4，因此该主教很快就会缺乏撤退方格。

事实上，在 10.0-0 之后，保留他的 Bb4 将是危险的，因为白方可能会发起旨在骚扰黑主教的攻击。例如，在游戏 Etchegaray - Sebban 中 10...Bb7？！ 11.Nb1 a5 12.a3 Bc5 13.Nc3 黑方以自然13...d6??自杀，并在战术序列14.b4之后！ axb4 15.axb4 Rxa1 16.Qxa1 Bxb4 17.Qa4+ Nc6 18.Nd5 白方胜一子。另一个例子是直接10...Bb7？！ 11.NF3！？不幸的是，黑方不能带着他的马，因为在 12...Nxf3 13.Bxf3 Bxf3 14.Qxf3 之后，他的 Ra8 和 c7 兵都会受到攻击。

因此，黑方必须将 Bb4 换成 Nd2。 10...Bxd2 11.Qxd2 Bb7 白方确实获得了节奏，因为他引发了 Bb4 与 Nd2 的交换，而无需玩 a2-a3。获得的这种节奏将使他能够在黑方建立防御以避免它之前实现 c4-c5 的推动。白棋可以用 b2-b4、Qc3 和/或 Rac1 准备推 c4-c5，例如：

在索洛任金 – 斯蒂亚日金（列宁格勒 1990）的比赛中，白棋尝试了立即牺牲 12.c5！？ bxc5 13.Qa5 及 13...d6 14.Bxe5 之后！ dxe5 15.Rfc1 白色的表现要好得多。然而，黑方在 Flear – Blatny（安道尔 1993 年）游戏中改进了这些棋步，立即以 13...Ng6 回还棋子！ 14.Qxc7 Nxf4 15.Qxf4 0-0，Lalic认为局势平衡。

12.Qc3 之后自然 12...d6!? 13.c5 bxc5 14.Bxe5 Qxe5 15.Qxe5+ dxe5 16.Rac1 0-0-0 17.Rxc5 领先后，白方取得了更好的结局，尽管拉利奇认为黑方应该坚持下去。因此，黑棋的另一种可能性是尝试不走 d7-d6，就像在 Gausel – Reite 游戏（挪威团体锦标赛，1991 年）中使用 12.Qc3 f6 13.b4 c5！？这是消除 c4-c5 威胁的根本方法。

在奥尔特曼-布拉特尼（Pardubice 1993）比赛中，怀特花时间准备c4-c5推，12.Rac1 d6 13.b4 0-0 14.c5 dxc5 15.bxc5 Rad8 16.Qc3 Ng6 17.Bg3 Rd5 18.cxb6 cxb6 19.Rfd1 Rfd8 20.Rxd5 Rxd5 21.a3 并且白方成功地释放了他的主教对，因此他有优势。因此，同一位黑人球员试图在 Chernin – Blatny（布尔诺 1993）比赛中提高自己的表现，立即撤退 13...Ng6，但在 14.Bg3 0-0 之后？！ 15.c5 dxc5 16.bxc5 Rfd8 17.Qb4 白方也占据主动。相反，Chernin 提出了一个完全不同的计划，即 14...h5!?，旨在迫使 Bg3 与 Ng6 交换，通过 h6 方格发展 Rh8，并将国王置于 f8 而不是易位。

黑棋以 9...0-0 放弃主教对

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Bf4 Nc6 5.Nf3 Bb4+ 6.Nbd2 Qe7 7.e3 Ngxe5 8.Nxe5 Nxe5 9.Be2 0-0

当黑棋选择 10...Bxd2 时，他面临着节奏比 7.a3 变体慢下来并很快无法应对白棋在后翼的位置威胁的风险。白棋可以避免推a2-a3并继续7.a3变化的标准计划。 Tseitlin 认为主要的变化是 9.Be2 d6 10.0-0 Bxd2 11.Qxd2 0-0 12.Rfd1 b6 13.b4 Bb7 14.c5 dxc5 15.bxc5，然后给出了他分析的一条线，其中黑方结束了棋子，但处于平局位置。同样，在走棋 9.Be2 Bxd2+ 10.Qxd2 d6 11.0-0 0-0 后，拉里克注意到：“通过在 d2 上如此早地交换并快速易位，黑方省去了如何与 Nb3 会面以及如何对待他的国王的担忧，但这种简单化的逻辑决不能保证他会玩得舒服。”

然而，一切对于黑方来说并没有那么糟糕。首先，为了实施他的计划，白棋必须集中精力发展（9.Be2，10.0-0），然后才能将注意力转向后翼。

explanations.pageTitle: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. c4/2...e5/3. dxe5/3...Ng4/4. Bf4/4...g5
explanations.text:
The sideline 4...g5!? was not well regarded at the end of the 20th century. Borik wrote that "the move 4...g5 creates irreparable weaknesses in Black's camp", while Tseitlin decided "this extravagant tactical stroke weakens the kingside and, on general ground alone, cannot be good". Lalic warned that "Black should be aware of the risks he is taking by playing such a line". Nonetheless, the 4...g5 line has found new supporters in recent years, thanks to Black's wins in Van Wely – Mamedyarov, Ciudad Real 2004 (where White played 5.Bg3), and Graf – Asik, Kavala 2007 (where White played 5.Bd2).

The main reason why 4...g5 was not well considered is that this move weakens a lot of squares, mostly f5 and h5 (as they cannot be covered by the g-pawn anymore). White can try to exploit these weaknesses with the manoeuvres Bf4–d2–c3 (pressure along the diagonal a1–h8), Ng1–e2–g3–h5 (pressure against the squares f6 and g7) and h2–h4 (to open the h-file).

The retreat 5.Bg3

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Bf4 g5 5.Bg3

For years, the reaction 5.Bg3 was not well considered because it does not make the most out of Black's provocative fourth move. Tseitlin considered that "the bishop is in danger of staying out of play for a long time". But later Lalic found that 5.Bg3 was "just as effective" as 5.Bd2. Black concentrates on getting his pawn back, while White tries to get an advantage from the weakening of the black kingside. After the possible 5...Bg7 6.Nf3 Nc6 7.Nc3 Ngxe5 8.Nxe5 Nxe5 9.e3 d6 White has tried several ideas:

After 10.h4 h6 Tseitlin considers that Black has a satisfactory game.

After the natural but inoffensive 10.Be2?! Be6 Tseitlin thinks Black already has equality.

White also tried 10.Rc1, to remove the latent positional threat Bxc3 (that would double White's queenside pawns), indirectly cover the c4-pawn, ease the c4–c5 push in a distant future notably if Black castles on the queenside). After 10...Be6 11.b3 h5!? 12.h4 Ng6 13.hxg5 Qxg5 Lalic assesses that "White must be fractionally better due to the potential weakness of Black's h-pawn".

Lalic considers the best try to be 10.c5!, sacrificing a pawn to weaken Black's control on the e5-square and expose the black king further. The game Fraschini – Fuentes (Cuba 1995) continued with 10...O-O 11.cxd6 cxd6 12.Be2 Qb6 13.Qd2 Be6 14.O-O and Black felt compelled to complicate things with 14...d5!? to avoid being slowly constricted on the d-file.

White has also tried to quickly open the h-file with 7.h4 Ngxe5 8.Nxe5 Nxe5 9.e3 but after 9...g4! Black succeeded in keeping the file closed.

The retreat 5.Bd2

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Bf4 g5 5.Bd2

The retreat 5.Bg3 is less considered than 5.Bd2 (in order to place the bishop on the wide-open diagonal a1–h8), after which "White can expect a safe advantage". Then according to Lalic delaying the recapture with 5...Bg7 6.Bc3 Nc6 7.e3 Ngxe5 is not correct as White can gain an advantage by 8.h4 or 8.Qh5, so the immediate 5...Nxe5 is better. For some time 6.Bc3 was well considered because Black had problems to deal with the various positional threats:

After 6...Bg7 7.e3 White already threatens to win a piece with the advance f2–f4. After 7...g4 8.Ne2 d6 9.Nf4 h5 10.Qc2 Joseph Staker suggests 10...Qg5 but play can continue by 11.Nd2 Bf5 12.Qb3 b6 13.c5! O-O 14.cxd6 cxd6 15.h4 Qh6 16.g3 Nbc6 17.Bg2 Rac8 18.O-O and White stands better thanks to the weaknesses in h5 and d6. Black has also tried 10...Na6 but it did not solve his problems.

After 6...Qe7 7.e3 Bg7?! White unleashes 8.h4! and Black has a creepy choice between 8...g4 (that would give the excellent f4-square for a white knight) and 8...h6 9.hxg5 hxg5 10.Rxh8+ Bxh8 11.Qh5 with advantage for White.

However the correct way for Black was found in 5...Nxe5 6.Bc3 Qe7 7.e3 Rg8! 8.Nf3 Nbc6 9.Be2 d6 10.Nd4 Bd7 11.b4 g4 with good counterplay for black on the kingside.

White's efforts then switched to 6.Nf3 to open the e-file, something that Black cannot really avoid as 6...Bg7 7.Nxe5 Bxe5 8.Bc3 would leave an advantage to White. For example 8...Qe7 9.Bxe5 10.Qxe5 10.Nc3 d6 11.e3 and Black is at a loss for an equalising line, White's advantage consisting in his ability to install his knight on the strong d5-square and to attack the weakened Black's kingside with the advance h2–h4. It is better for Black to continue with 6...Nxf3+ 7.exf3 when both 7...h5? and 7...Bg7 would fail to 8.Qe2+, so Black must try 7...d6 8.Qe2+ Be6 instead.

explanations.textZh:
边线4...g5！？在20世纪末并没有得到很好的重视。博里克（Borik）写道，“4...g5 棋给黑方阵营造成了无法弥补的弱点”，而特塞特林（Tseitlin）则认为“这种奢侈的战术打击削弱了王翼，仅从一般情况来看，这不会是好事”。拉利奇警告说，“黑方应该意识到他走这样的路线所面临的风险”。尽管如此，4...g5线近年来找到了新的支持者，这要归功于黑方在2004年范韦利-马梅迪亚罗夫、雷阿尔城（白方下棋5.Bg3）和2007年格拉夫-阿西克、卡瓦拉（白方下棋5.Bd2）中的胜利。

4...g5 没有被充分考虑的主要原因是，这一举动削弱了很多方格，主要是 f5 和 h5（因为它们不再被 g-pawn 覆盖）。白方可以尝试利用 Bf4–d2–c3（沿对角线 a1–h8 施压）、Ng1–e2–g3–h5（对方格 f6 和 g7 施压）和 h2–h4（打开 h 文件）来利用这些弱点。

撤退5.Bg3

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 NG4 4.Bf4 g5 5.Bg3

多年来，反应 5.Bg3 没有得到充分考虑，因为它没有充分利用黑方的挑衅性第四步棋。特塞特林认为“主教有长期缺席比赛的危险”。但后来 Lalic 发现 5.Bg3 与 5.Bd2“一样有效”。黑方集中精力夺回棋子，而白方则试图从黑方王翼的削弱中获得优势。在可能的 5...Bg7 6.Nf3 Nc6 7.Nc3 Ngxe5 8.Nxe5 Nxe5 9.e3 d6 之后，白棋尝试了几种想法：

10.h4 h6 后，Tseitlin 认为黑棋的棋局令人满意。

在自然但无害的10.Be2之后？！ Be6 Tseitlin 认为黑方已经平等。

白方还尝试了 10.Rc1，以消除潜在的位置威胁 Bxc3（这将使白方的后侧棋子加倍），间接覆盖 c4 棋子，在遥远的将来缓解 c4-c5 的推动，特别是如果黑方在后侧城堡的话）。 10之后...Be6 11.b3 h5！？ 12.h4 Ng6 13.hxg5 Qxg5 Lalic 评估“由于黑方 h 兵的潜在弱点，白棋一定稍好一些”。

Lalic 认为最好的尝试是 10.c5！，牺牲一个棋子来削弱黑方对 e5 方格的控制并进一步暴露黑王。 Fraschini – Fuentes 比赛（古巴 1995 年）继续进行 10...O-O 11.cxd6 cxd6 12.Be2 Qb6 13.Qd2 Be6 14.O-O，黑方感到有必要用 14...d5 让事情变得复杂！？以避免被慢慢限制在 d 文件上。

White还尝试使用7.h4 Ngxe5 8.Nxe5 Nxe5 9.e3快速打开h文件，但在9...g4之后！布莱克成功地关闭了档案。

撤退5.Bd2

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 NG4 4.Bf4 g5 5.Bd2

撤退 5.Bg3 比 5.Bd2 更少被考虑（为了将象放置在敞开的对角线 a1-h8 上），此后“白棋可以期待安全优势”。然后根据 Lalic，用 5...Bg7 6.Bc3 Nc6 7.e3 Ngxe5 延迟夺回是不正确的，因为白方可以通过 8.h4 或 8.Qh5 获得优势，因此立即的 5...Nxe5 更好。一段时间以来，6.Bc3 被充分考虑，因为黑方在应对各种位置威胁方面存在问题：

6...Bg7 7.e3 之后，白棋已经威胁要通过前进 f2-f4 赢得棋子。 7...g4 8.Ne2 d6 9.Nf4 h5 10.Qc2 之后 Joseph Staker 建议 10...Qg5 但比赛可以继续进行 11.Nd2 Bf5 12.Qb3 b6 13.c5！ O-O 14.cxd6 cxd6 15.h4 Qh6 16.g3 Nbc6 17.Bg2 Rac8 18.O-O 和白棋由于 h5 和 d6 的弱点而表现更好。黑方也尝试过 10...Na6 但并没有解决他的问题。

6...Qe7 7.e3 Bg7 之后？！白方释放 8.h4！黑棋在 8...g4（这将为白马提供出色的 f4 方格）和 8...h6 9.hxg5 hxg5 10.Rxh8+ Bxh8 11.Qh5 之间有一个令人毛骨悚然的选择，白棋有优势。

然而，黑棋的正确走法是在 5...Nxe5 6.Bc3 Qe7 7.e3 Rg8 中找到的！ 8.Nf3 Nbc6 9.Be2 d6 10.Nd4 Bd7 11.b4 g4 在王翼对黑棋有很好的反击作用。

然后白方的努力转向 6.Nf3 打开电子文件，这是黑方无法真正避免的，因为 6...Bg7 7.Nxe5 Bxe5 8.Bc3 会给白方留下优势。例如8...Qe7 9.Bxe5 10.Qxe5 10.Nc3 d6 11.e3，黑方在均衡线中不知所措，白方的优势在于他有能力将他的骑士安置在强大的d5方格上，并通过前进h2-h4攻击被削弱的黑方王翼。当双方都是 7...h5 时，黑方继续下 6...Nxf3+ 7.exf3 更好吗？ 7...Bg7 无法下 8.Qe2+，因此黑棋必须尝试 7...d6 8.Qe2+ Be6。

笔记

explanations.pageTitle: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. c4/2...e5/3. dxe5/3...Ng4/4. e4
explanations.text:
Variations

This variation is named after Alexander Alekhine probably thanks to his wins in the games Alekhine – Rabinovic (Baden Baden, 1925) and Alekhine – Seitz (Hastings, 1926). Alekhine himself stated:

This is considered with good reason to be White's best system against the Budapest Gambit. White hands the pawn back, but in return gains control of d5. Over the next few moves, however, he has to play with extreme precision, since otherwise his central pawn position may become the object of a successful attack by Black.

White does not try to keep its material advantage (the e5-pawn) and concentrates on building a strong pawn centre, in order to get a space advantage. Notably a controversial point is whether the typical black manoeuvre Bf8–b4–xc3 is advantageous for Black (as it saddles White with doubled pawns) or for White (as it reinforces his centre). Lalic thinks both, considering 6...Bb4+ to be a bad move after 4...Nxe5 5.f4 Nec6 6.Nf3, but a good one after 4...Nxe5 5.f4 Nec6 6.Be3.

After 4.e4 Black has to do something about its Ng4 that is attacked by the Qd1. Apart from the main line, two minor variations have been tried:

with 4...h5?! Black does not want to get its gambit pawn back, and prefers to keep the Ng4 on its aggressive position. Thus White has to be careful not to fall in some traps like 5.Nf3? Bc5 or 5.f4?! Bc5 6.Nh3 Nc6 7.Be2? Qh4+. White does best to repel immediately the Ng4 with 5.Be2, after which the move h7–h5 is only a weakness and White has the advantage.

with 4...d6?! Black continues in true gambit style, trying to develop rapidly its pieces, but the compensations are not sufficient. Here again, after 5.exd6 Bxd6 White needs to avoid some traps like 6.Nf3? Bc5! 7.Qxd8+ Kxd8 when Black regains the pawn with advantage. White continues with 6.Be2 to gain a tempo on the Ng4 when Black's only option to sustain an initiative is 6...f5 7.exf5 Qe7. Then White has a choice between chasing a slight positional advantage with 8.Nf3, or taking a piece with 8.c5! Bxc5 9.Qa4+ Nc6 10.Qxg4. In the later case, Savielly Tartakower and Max Euwe initially considered Black had enough compensation but more recent analysis proved them wrong.

The main line is 4...Nxe5 5.f4 when Black has an important choice to make about where to move its Ne5:

5...Nec6 is considered to be the best

5...Ng6 is probably playable

5...Nbc6? 6.fxe5 Qh4+, despite being called "highly regarded" by Lalic, is just a bad piece sacrifice with Black hoping for something like 7.g3? Qe4+ that wins a rook. As advocated by John Nunn White can keep the material advantage with the funny 7.Kd2 Qf4+ 8.Kc3 Qxe5+ 9.Kd2 Qf4+ 10.Ke1 Qxe4+ 11.Qe2 when the black queen is pinned.

The 5...Nec6 line

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.e4 Nxe5 5.f4 Nec6

The Knight on c6 is safer than on g6, and can be part of a general strategy on the dark squares. It can go on d4 while the other Knight can go on c5 via a6 or d7.

After 6.Nf3 Bc5 White has difficulties to castle short, because the plan to exchange the dark-squared bishops with Bd3/Qe2/Be3 can be met by Bg4/Nd4 in order to muddy the waters. Therefore, as Lalic points out:

White can no longer castle kingside and will usually have to go the other way. However, this is rather slow and gives Black time to try and undermine the white centre. To this end Bc8–g4 often comes in handy, in order to pin the white knight on f3 against the white queen. Note that Black should wait until his opponent has wasted a tempo with Qe2.

A possible continuation is 6.Nf3 Bc5 7.Nc3 d6 8.f5!? Nd7 9.Bg5 f6 10.Bf4 and here Black has to prepare the exchange of the Bc5 against the Nc3 with 10...Bb4!, because a White knight on the d5-square would be too strong now that it cannot be challenged by Bc8–e6 and it can continue with Nd5–f4–e6 in the long run. A slower course of action is 6.Nf3 Bc5 7.Nc3 d6 8.Bd3 O-O 9.Qe2 Bg4! 10.Be3 Na6 11.O-O-O f6 with a typical game of opposite castles. White cannot, however, afford the luxury of being too slow, e.g. after 6.Nf3 Bc5 7.Nc3 d6 8.Bd3 O-O 9.h3?! Re8 it is already time for White to seek a simplification with 10.Qe2 Nd4 11.Nxd4 Bxd4 12.Be3 Qh4+ 13.Qf2, otherwise Black would soon have strong pressure in the centre thanks to the semi-open e-file.

Another try is 6.a3 but it creates a significant weakness in b3 and it is rather slow. For example after the possible 6...a5 7.Be3 Na6 8.Bd3 Bc5 9.Qd2 d6 10.Nf3 O-O 11.Nc3 Bxe3 12.Qxe3 Nc5 13.O-O Re8 14.Bc2 a4 Borik has shown that the possibility to attack the c4-pawn with Be6/Na5 gives sufficient play to Black. Note that Black is not compelled to reply to 6.a3 with 6...a5, and can also treat a2–a3 as a mere loss of tempo by switching to another development like d6/g6/Bg7/O-O with equality. As Lalic puts it:

[I] believe that Black should now opt for the plan of fianchettoing his dark-squared bishop. The black bishop will be excellently posted on g7 and Black's kingside will also be more robust against White's eventual kingside attack.

Over the next few moves, however, he has to play with extreme precision, since otherwise his central pawn position may become the object of a successful attack by Black.

White does not try to keep its material advantage (the e5-pawn) and concentrates on building a strong pawn centre, in order to get a space advantage. Notably a controversial point is whether the typical black manoeuvre Bf8–b4–xc3 is advantageous for Black (as it saddles White with doubled pawns) or for White (as it reinforces his centre). Lalic thinks both, considering 6...Bb4+ to be a bad move after 4...Nxe5 5.f4 Nec6 6.Nf3, but a good one after 4...Nxe5 5.f4 Nec6 6.Be3.

After 4.e4 Black has to do something about its Ng4 that is attacked by the Qd1. Apart from the main line, two minor variations have been tried:

with 4...h5?! Black does not want to get its gambit pawn back, and prefers to keep the Ng4 on its aggressive position. Thus White has to be careful not to fall in some traps like 5.Nf3? Bc5 or 5.f4?! Bc5 6.Nh3 Nc6 7.Be2? Qh4+. White does best to repel immediately the Ng4 with 5.Be2, after which the move h7–h5 is only a weakness and White has the advantage.

with 4...d6?! Black continues in true gambit style, trying to develop rapidly its pieces, but the compensations are not sufficient. Here again, after 5.exd6 Bxd6 White needs to avoid some traps like 6.Nf3? Bc5! 7.Qxd8+ Kxd8 when Black regains the pawn with advantage. White continues with 6.Be2 to gain a tempo on the Ng4 when Black's only option to sustain an initiative is 6...f5 7.exf5 Qe7. Then White has a choice between chasing a slight positional advantage with 8.Nf3, or taking a piece with 8.c5! Bxc5 9.Qa4+ Nc6 10.Qxg4. In the later case, Savielly Tartakower and Max Euwe initially considered Black had enough compensation but more recent analysis proved them wrong.

The main line is 4...Nxe5 5.f4 when Black has an important choice to make about where to move its Ne5:

5...Nec6 is considered to be the best

5...Ng6 is probably playable

5...Nbc6? 6.fxe5 Qh4+, despite being called "highly regarded" by Lalic, is just a bad piece sacrifice with Black hoping for something like 7.g3? Qe4+ that wins a rook. As advocated by John Nunn White can keep the material advantage with the funny 7.Kd2 Qf4+ 8.Kc3 Qxe5+ 9.Kd2 Qf4+ 10.Ke1 Qxe4+ 11.Qe2 when the black queen is pinned.

The 5...Nec6 line

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.e4 Nxe5 5.f4 Nec6

The Knight on c6 is safer than on g6, and can be part of a general strategy on the dark squares. It can go on d4 while the other Knight can go on c5 via a6 or d7.

After 6.Nf3 Bc5 White has difficulties to castle short, because the plan to exchange the dark-squared bishops with Bd3/Qe2/Be3 can be met by Bg4/Nd4 in order to muddy the waters. Therefore, as Lalic points out:

White can no longer castle kingside and will usually have to go the other way. However, this is rather slow and gives Black time to try and undermine the white centre. To this end Bc8–g4 often comes in handy, in order to pin the white knight on f3 against the white queen. Note that Black should wait until his opponent has wasted a tempo with Qe2.

A possible continuation is 6.Nf3 Bc5 7.Nc3 d6 8.f5!? Nd7 9.Bg5 f6 10.Bf4 and here Black has to prepare the exchange of the Bc5 against the Nc3 with 10...Bb4!, because a White knight on the d5-square would be too strong now that it cannot be challenged by Bc8–e6 and it can continue with Nd5–f4–e6 in the long run. A slower course of action is 6.Nf3 Bc5 7.Nc3 d6 8.Bd3 O-O 9.Qe2 Bg4! 10.Be3 Na6 11.O-O-O f6 with a typical game of opposite castles. White cannot, however, afford the luxury of being too slow, e.g. after 6.Nf3 Bc5 7.Nc3 d6 8.Bd3 O-O 9.h3?! Re8 it is already time for White to seek a simplification with 10.Qe2 Nd4 11.Nxd4 Bxd4 12.Be3 Qh4+ 13.Qf2, otherwise Black would soon have strong pressure in the centre thanks to the semi-open e-file.

Another try is 6.a3 but it creates a significant weakness in b3 and it is rather slow. For example after the possible 6...a5 7.Be3 Na6 8.Bd3 Bc5 9.Qd2 d6 10.Nf3 O-O 11.Nc3 Bxe3 12.Qxe3 Nc5 13.O-O Re8 14.Bc2 a4 Borik has shown that the possibility to attack the c4-pawn with Be6/Na5 gives sufficient play to Black. Note that Black is not compelled to reply to 6.a3 with 6...a5, and can also treat a2–a3 as a mere loss of tempo by switching to another development like d6/g6/Bg7/O-O with equality. As Lalic puts it:

[I] believe that Black should now opt for the plan of fianchettoing his dark-squared bishop. The black bishop will be excellently posted on g7 and Black's kingside will also be more robust against White's eventual kingside attack.
explanations.textZh:
变化

这种变化以亚历山大·阿廖欣 (Alexander Alekhine) 的名字命名，可能是由于他在阿廖欣 - 拉比诺维奇 (巴登巴登，1925 年) 和阿廖欣 - 塞茨 (黑斯廷斯，1926 年) 比赛中获胜。阿廖欣本人说道：

这有充分的理由被认为是白方对抗布达佩斯弃兵的最佳系统。白棋将棋子交还给棋子，但作为回报获得了 d5 的控制权。然而，在接下来的几步棋中，他必须走得极其精确，否则他的中心棋子位置可能会成为黑方成功攻击的目标。

白棋并没有试图保持其物质优势（e5兵），而是集中精力建立一个强大的兵中心，以获得空间优势。值得注意的是，一个有争议的问题是，典型的黑棋策略 Bf8-b4-xc3 是否对黑方有利（因为它给白方带来了双兵），或者对白方有利（因为它加强了白方的中心）。 Lalic 两者都认为，认为 4...Nxe5 5.f4 Nec6 6.Nf3 之后 6...Bb4+ 是一个糟糕的举动，但在 4...Nxe5 5.f4 Nec6 6.Be3 之后是一个好的举动。

4.e4 之后，黑方必须对其受到 Qd1 攻击的 Ng4 采取一些措施。除了主线之外，还尝试了两个小的变化：

4...h5？！黑方不想拿回其开局棋子，并且更愿意将 Ng4 保持在进攻位置。因此白棋必须小心，不要落入5.Nf3之类的陷阱？ BC5 还是 5.f4？！ Bc5 6.Nh3 Nc6 7.Be2？ Qh4+。白棋最好立即用 5.Be2 击退 Ng4，之后 h7-h5 棋只是弱点，白棋具有优势。

与 4...d6？！黑方继续以真正的策略风格，试图快速发展其棋子，但补偿不足。再说一遍，在 5.exd6 Bxd6 之后，白方需要避免一些像 6.Nf3 这样的陷阱吗？ BC5！ 7.Qxd8+ Kxd8，当黑方以优势夺回棋子时。白方继续下 6.Be2 以在 Ng4 上获得节奏，而黑方维持主动的唯一选择是 6...f5 7.exf5 Qe7。那么白棋就可以选择是用 8.Nf3 追逐稍微的位置优势，还是用 8.c5 拿下棋子！ Bxc5 9.Qa4+ Nc6 10.Qxg4。在后一个案例中，萨维利·塔塔科维尔和马克斯·尤威最初认为布莱克有足够的补偿，但最近的分析证明他们错了。

主线是 4...Nxe5 5.f4，此时黑方需要做出重要选择，决定将其 Ne5 移至何处：

5...Nec6被认为是最好的

5...NG6 可能可以玩

5...NBC6？ 6.fxe5 Qh4+，尽管被Lalic称为“高度重视”，但只是一个糟糕的棋子牺牲，黑方希望得到像7.g3这样的东西？ Qe4+ 赢得车。正如约翰·纳恩（John Nunn）所主张的那样，当黑后被牵制时，怀特可以用有趣的 7.Kd2 Qf4+ 8.Kc3 Qxe5+ 9.Kd2 Qf4+ 10.Ke1 Qxe4+ 11.Qe2 保持物质优势。

5...Nec6 线

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 NG4 4.e4 Nxe5 5.f4 Nec6

c6 上的骑士比 g6 上的骑士更安全，并且可以成为黑暗方块上一般策略的一部分。它可以继续 d4，而另一个骑士可以通过 a6 或 d7 继续 c5。

6.Nf3 Bc5之后，白方很难短兵相接，因为用Bd3/Qe2/Be3交换暗方主教的计划可能会被Bg4/Nd4满足，从而搅浑水。因此，正如拉利克所指出的：

白方不能再在王侧筑城，通常必须走另一条路。然而，这是相当缓慢的，给了黑方时间来尝试破坏白方中心。为此，Bc8-g4 经常派上用场，以便将 f3 上的白马钉住对抗白后。请注意，黑棋应该等到对手用 Qe2 浪费了节奏。

可能的延续是 6.Nf3 Bc5 7.Nc3 d6 8.f5!? Nd7 9.Bg5 f6 10.Bf4，这里黑方必须准备 Bc5 与 Nc3 与 10...Bb4 的交换！，因为 d5 方格上的白马现在太强大了，无法被 Bc8–e6 挑战，从长远来看，它可以继续 Nd5–f4–e6。较慢的行动方针是 6.Nf3 Bc5 7.Nc3 d6 8.Bd3 O-O 9.Qe2 Bg4！ 10.Be3 Na6 11.O-O-O f6 具有典型的相反城堡游戏。然而，白棋不能承受太慢的奢侈，例如6.Nf3 Bc5 7.Nc3 d6 8.Bd3 O-O 9.h3 之后？！ Re8已经到了白棋寻求简化的时候了，10.Qe2 Nd4 11.Nxd4 Bxd4 12.Be3 Qh4+ 13.Qf2，否则黑棋很快就会在半开电子档的作用下在中路受到强大的压力。

另一种尝试是 6.a3，但它在 b3 中造成了明显的弱点，而且速度相当慢。例如，在可能的 6...a5 7.Be3 Na6 8.Bd3 Bc5 9.Qd2 d6 10.Nf3 O-O 11.Nc3 Bxe3 12.Qxe3 Nc5 13.O-O Re8 14.Bc2 a4 Borik 已经表明，用 Be6/Na5 攻击 c4 兵的可能性为黑方提供了足够的发挥空间。请注意，黑方不必用 6...a5 来回应 6.a3，并且也可以通过平等地切换到 d6/g6/Bg7/O-O 等其他发展，将 a2–a3 视为仅仅是节奏损失。正如拉利克所说：

[我]相信布莱克现在应该选择对他的黑方主教进行劈砍的计划。黑象将在 g7 中表现出色，并且黑棋的王翼也将更强大地对抗白棋最终的王翼进攻。

explanations.pageTitle: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. c4/2...e5/3. dxe5/3...Ng4/4. Nf3
explanations.text:
Adler variation

The Adler variation is named after the game Adler – Maróczy which was played at the 1896 Budapest tournament. White is ready to give up the e5-pawn in order to develop all their pieces on their best squares, i.e. the d5-square for the Nb1, the f3-square for the Ng1 and the a1–h8 diagonal for the Bc1.

In the main line 4...Bc5 the f2-pawn is attacked, forcing 5.e3 that blocks the way for the Bc1. Then after 5...Nc6 White has not enough pieces to protect their e5-pawn on the long run, e.g.:

6.Qd5?! is a doomed attempt, exposing the queen and occupying the d5-square that should belong to the Nb1. This move has a historical interest as this was the line played in the first game where the Budapest Gambit occurred. Black continues calmly with Qe7/Ngxe5/d6/Be6.

6.Bd2 O-O 7.Nc3 Qe7 does not prevent Black to regain their pawn either, and it obstructs the way to the d5-square for the Nb1. Once they have the pawn back Black has equality.

6.b3 immediately allows Black to play 6...d6! when White cannot capture in d6 because of Qd8–f6 winning the Ra1. Play will likely transpose into the 6.Be2 variation.

An important theoretical decision for White is to choose whether they wants to make a2–a3 part of their plan or not. While this move avoids any possible Nc6–b4 and creates the possibility b2–b4, it may also be seen as a possible waste of time in some lines. As Lalic puts it:It was not so long ago that 8.a3, with the obvious intention of expanding with b2–b4, was the standard move. However, after Black responds with the logical a7–a5, it became apparent in tournament practice that the inclusion of these moves is in fact in Black's favour, as it gives their queen's rook access into play via the a6-square.

Black can also try the minor line /4...Nc6/ that allows Black to delay the development of the f8-diagonal depending on the circumstances, and allows White to transpose into the 4.Bf4 variation if they wish to do so.

The 4...Bc5 line with a2–a3

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Nf3 Bc5 5.e3 Nc6 6.a3

After the standard moves 6...a5 7.b3 O-O 8.Bb2 Re8 9.Nc3 Ngxe5 10.Nxe5 Nxe5 11.Be2 d6 12.O-O both kings are in safety and Black has regained the invested pawn in the process. Both players can deviate at various points but the positions reached are similar, e.g. in one game White played an early Ra1–b1 in order to push b2–b4 in one move, but Black continued with the same plan as explained hereunder. In another game White developed their Bf1 in d3 instead of e2, but this gave the opportunity for Black to sacrifice the Ng4 on the f2-pawn before the white castle.

White has a space advantage in the center and can initiate pressure here or on the queenside by some pawn pushes like b3–b4 and c4–c5 (possibly supported by a knight on the d5-square). Meanwhile, the White king lacks some defenders so Black can start a pieces-driven attack with the standard "rook lift". As Tseitlin puts it, "the point is that 6...a5 fits into the plan of attacking White's kingside (!), whereas 6.a3 does little in the way of defending it". Thus if White does not find a clear way to make good use of their move a2–a3, it may turn out to be a waste of tempo.

After 12...Re6 White has to chose a way to react to the oncoming assault:

13.Nd5 Rh6 14.g3 (to avoid the crushing 14...Qh4) 14...Bh3 15.Re1 when the Nd5 seems excellently placed, supporting the b3–b4 push on the queenside and one jump away from the f4-square where it can cover the weak light squares h3 and g2 if needed. Nevertheless, after 15...c6!? 16.Nf4 Bf5 it may be difficult for White to realise the b3–b4 push and the weakness of the d6-pawn is not of great significance as long as White cannot attack it with their minor pieces, so chances are level. Thus placing the Nc3 in d5 may be premature.

13.g3 Rh6 14.Ne4 seems crushing as White threatens to win both the Bc5 and the Ne5 (the d6-pawn is pinned). Moreover the Ne4 is well placed to support a later c4–c5 push. Black must react with 14...Qd7 in order to get out of the pin and continue the initiative. Now White has to lose a tempo and weaken their kingside further with 15.h4 in order to avoid the terrific threat Qh3–Qxh2#. After 15...Ba7 Black has dynamic equality.

13.Na4 is another try for White, hindering Re6–h6 because of Bxe5. Black must switch to defence on the queenside with 13...b6!? 14.Nxc5 bxc5 15.f4 (necessary to improve the prospects of the Be2) Nd7 16.Bf3 Rb8 17.Qd3 a4! when Black is even better. In this plan it is important that Black does not fear to move their imprisoned Bc5, e.g. 14.Bc3 (threatening 15.b4) 14...Bd7 15.b4? Bxa4 16.Qxa4 axb4.

The 4...Bc5 line without a2–a3

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Nf3 Bc5 5.e3 Nc6

In this variation White reasons that the advance a2–a3 is only a loss of time, because Black will play a7–a5 anyway. By refraining from the advance a2-a3 White tries to gain a tempo on the lines of the previous section, to make it more difficult for Black to initiate the Re8–e6–h6 lift.

explanations.textZh:
阿德勒变体

Adler 变体以 1896 年布达佩斯锦标赛上进行的 Adler – Maróczy 游戏命名。白方准备放弃 e5 兵，以便将所有棋子部署在其最佳方格上，即 Nb1 的 d5 方格、Ng1 的 f3 方格和 Bc1 的 a1-h8 对角线。

在主线 4...Bc5 中，f2-pawn 受到攻击，迫使 5.e3 挡住了 Bc1 的道路。然后在 5...Nc6 之后，白方没有足够的棋子来长期保护他们的 e5 兵，例如：

6.Qd5？！这是一次注定失败的尝试，暴露了皇后并占领了本应属于Nb1的d5方格。这一举动具有历史意义，因为这是布达佩斯弃兵发生的第一场比赛中所使用的路线。黑棋继续平静地下Qe7/Ngxe5/d6/Be6。

6.Bd2 O-O 7.Nc3 Qe7 也不能阻止黑方夺回棋子，并且它阻碍了 Nb1 通往 d5 方格的道路。一旦他们拿回棋子，黑棋就平等了。

6.b3 立即允许黑方下 6...d6！当白方在 d6 中无法吃子时，因为 Qd8-f6 赢得了 Ra1。 Play 可能会转入 6.Be2 变体。

白棋的一个重要的理论决策是选择是否要将 a2-a3 纳入其计划中。虽然这一举动避免了任何可能的 Nc6-b4 并创造了 b2-b4 的可能性，但在某些行中它也可能被视为可能浪费时间。正如 Lalic 所说：不久前，8.a3 是标准走法，其明显的意图是通过 b2-b4 进行扩展。然而，在黑方用符合逻辑的a7-a5做出回应后，在锦标赛实践中很明显，这些棋步的包含实际上对黑方有利，因为它使他们的后车可以通过a6方格进入游戏。

黑方还可以尝试次要线/4...Nc6/，它允许黑方根据情况延迟f8对角线的发展，并允许白方如果愿意的话可以转入4.Bf4变体。

4...Bc5 线与 a2–a3

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 NG4 4.Nf3 Bc5 5.e3 Nc6 6.a3

标准走法 6...a5 7.b3 O-O 8.Bb2 Re8 9.Nc3 Ngxe5 10.Nxe5 Nxe5 11.Be2 d6 12.O-O 后，两位国王都处于安全状态，黑方在此过程中重新获得了投入的棋子。两名球员可能会在不同的点上出现偏差，但达到的位置是相似的，例如在一场比赛中，白棋早期出 Ra1-b1，以便一步推动 b2-b4，但黑棋继续执行与下文所述相同的计划。在另一场比赛中，白方在 d3 中开发了 Bf1 而不是 e2，但这给了黑方在白方城堡之前牺牲 f2 兵上的 Ng4 的机会。

白方在中心具有空间优势，可以通过 b3-b4 和 c4-c5 等推兵（可能由 d5 方格上的马支持）在这里或后侧发起压力。与此同时，白王缺少一些防守者，因此黑方可以使用标准的“车举”发起以棋子驱动的进攻。正如 Tseitlin 所说，“重点是 6...a5 符合攻击白方王翼的计划（！），而 6.a3 在防守方面几乎没有什么作用”。因此，如果白棋没有找到一个明确的方法来充分利用他们的a2-a3步棋，结果可能会浪费节奏。

12...Re6 白方必须选择一种方式来应对即将到来的攻击：

13.Nd5 Rh6 14.g3（避免压碎14...Qh4） 14...Bh3 15.Re1 当Nd5看起来位置极佳时，支持后侧的b3-b4推力，并从f4方格跳开，如果需要，它可以覆盖弱光方格h3和g2。尽管如此，15...c6之后！？ 16.Nf4 Bf5 白棋可能很难实现b3-b4推，只要白棋不能用小子攻击d6兵，d6兵的弱点并不重要，所以机会是平等的。因此将 Nc3 放入 d5 可能为时过早。

13.g3 Rh6 14.Ne4 似乎具有压倒性，因为白方威胁要赢得 Bc5 和 Ne5（d6 兵已被固定）。此外，Ne4 可以很好地支持后来的 c4-c5 推送。黑棋必须用 14...Qd7 做出反应，才能脱离平局并继续占据主动。现在，白方必须失去节奏，并通过 15.h4 进一步削弱其王翼，以避免可怕的威胁 Qh3–Qxh2#。 15...Ba7 黑之后动态相等。

13.Na4是白方的另一次尝试，由于Bxe5阻碍了Re6–h6。黑方必须以 13...b6 转为后翼防守！？ 14.Nxc5 bxc5 15.f4（改善Be2前景必备） Nd7 16.Bf3 Rb8 17.Qd3 a4！当黑棋更好时。在这个计划中，重要的是黑方不要害怕移动他们被囚禁的 Bc5，例如14.Bc3（威胁15.b4）14...Bd7 15.b4？ Bxa4 16.Qxa4 axb4。

没有 a2–a3 的 4...Bc5 行

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Nf3 Bc5 5.e3 Nc6

在这个变体中，白棋认为前进a2-a3只是浪费时间，因为黑棋无论如何都会下a7-a5。通过避免前进a2-a3，白方试图获得前一部分的节奏，使黑方更难启动Re8-e6-h6 提升。

explanations.pageTitle: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. c4/2...e5/3. dxe5/3...Ng4/4. Nf3/4...Nc6
explanations.text:
The 4...Nc6 line

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Nf3 Nc6

Black plays this when he wants to postpone the placement of its dark-squared bishop. Now White has a wide choice:

5.Bf4 transposes in the 4.Bf4 variation explained hereafter.

5.Qd5 transposes in the minor line 4.Qd5 explained hereafter.

5.Nc3 will transpose into the 4...Bc5 line if Black plays 5...Bc5, but Black can also wait a bit to see what White is up to, e.g. 5...Ngxe5 6.Nxe5 Nxe5 7.Qc2 Bb4 when both players are still hesitating to castle long or short.

5.e3 Bb4+

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.e3 Bb4+

After 5.e3 the check 5...Bb4+ is not that good because White can react with the simple 6.Bd2 that does not concede anything and keeps the possibility for his Nb1 to reach the important d5-square. A game continued 6...Bxd2+ 7.Qxd2 O-O 8.Be2 Ncxe5 9.Nxe5 Nxe5 10.O-O d6 11.Nc3 Bg4 12.f3 Be6 13.b3 Qh4 and here Borik advises 14.Nd5 with the more comfortable game.

The other reply 6.Nc3 is good only if Black makes the errors of not doubling White's pawns with the immediate 6...Bxc3+. For example in a game after 6...Ngxe5 7.Bd2 O-O 8.a3! Bxc3 9.Bxc3 d6 Black had no compensation for the loss of the bishop pair. After the correct 6...Bxc3+ 7.bxc3 Qe7! (important to prevent both c4–c5 and Bc1–a3) 8.a4 Ngxe5 9.Ba3 d6 10.c5 Nxf3+ 11.gxf3 Qe5! 12.Qd2 dxc5 and White had not sufficient compensation for the pawn.

5.e3 Ngxe5

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.e3 Ngxe5

Better for Black is 5...Ngxe5 when Black can go into a kind of King's Indian Defence setup with g7–g6 and Bf8–g7. Then the pressure along the a1–h8 diagonal can be enhanced via the quick advance a7–a5–a4–a3. For example after 5.e3 Ngxe5 6.Be2 g6 ("!?" Lalic) 7.O-O Bg7 8.Nc3 O-O 9.Qd2 d6 10.h3 ("?" Lalic) 10...a5 ("!" Lalic) 11.b3 a4 and now 12.Bb2 would have been followed by 12.a3! 13.Bc1 Nxf3+ 14.Bxf3 Qf6 winning the Nc3.

5.Bg5

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.Bg5

5.Bg5 Be7 6.Bxe7 (6.Bf4 Bb4+ transposes in the 4.Bf4 variation) 6...Qxe7 7.Nc3 with the dangerous positional threat Nc3–d5. Here Borik advocates 7...Qc5 8.e3 Ngxe5, when he can react to Qd1–d5 with Qc5–e7 (and the d5-square is no more available to the Nc3), and to Nc3–d5 with Nc6–e7 (to exchange the annoying knight). Black can also delay the recapture of the e5-pawn with 7...O-O 8.Nd5 Qd8 9.e3 Ngxe5 10.Nxe5 Nxe5. Meanwhile, the natural 7...Ngxe5 falls into White's positional trap and after 8.Nd5 ("!?" Lalic) 8...Qd8 9.Nxe5 Nxe5 10.Qd4 f6 11.f4 Ng6 12.Qe4+ Kf7 White got an edge.

explanations.textZh:
4...Nc6 线

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 NG4 4.Nf3 Nc6

当黑方想推迟放置暗方象时，他可以下此棋。现在白棋有多种选择：

5.Bf4 在下文解释的 4.Bf4 变体中转置。

5.Qd5 在小行中转置 4.Qd5 解释如下。

如果黑方下 5...Bc5，5.Nc3 将转入 4...Bc5 线，但黑方也可以稍等一下，看看白方在做什么，例如5...Ngxe5 6.Nxe5 Nxe5 7.Qc2 Bb4，当双方玩家还在犹豫是做多还是做空时。

5.e3 Bb4+

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Ng4 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.e3 Bb4+

5.e3 之后，检查 5...Bb4+ 不太好，因为白方可以用简单的 6.Bd2 做出反应，不会让步，并保留他的 Nb1 到达重要 d5 方格的可能性。比赛继续进行 6...Bxd2+ 7.Qxd2 O-O 8.Be2 Ncxe5 9.Nxe5 Nxe5 10.O-O d6 11.Nc3 Bg4 12.f3 Be6 13.b3 Qh4 在这里，Borik 建议 14.Nd5 进行更舒适的比赛。

仅当黑方犯了没有用直接 6...Bxc3+ 加倍白方棋子的错误时，另一个答复 6.Nc3 才是好的。例如，在 6...Ngxe5 7.Bd2 O-O 8.a3 之后的游戏中！ Bxc3 9.Bxc3 d6 黑方对于失去象对没有任何补偿。正确后 6...Bxc3+ 7.bxc3 Qe7！ （对于防止 c4–c5 和 Bc1–a3 很重要） 8.a4 Ngxe5 9.Ba3 d6 10.c5 Nxf3+ 11.gxf3 Qe5！ 12.Qd2 dxc5 和白棋没有足够的棋子补偿。

5.e3 ngxe5

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 NG4 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.e3 Ngxe5

对于黑方来说更好的是 5...Ngxe5，此时黑方可以使用 g7–g6 和 Bf8–g7 进入国王的印度防御设置。然后，可以通过快速推进a7-a5-a4-a3来增强沿a1-h8对角线的压力。例如，在 5.e3 Ngxe5 6.Be2 g6 ("!?" Lalic) 7.O-O Bg7 8.Nc3 O-O 9.Qd2 d6 10.h3 ("?" Lalic) 10...a5 ("!" Lalic) 11.b3 a4 之后，现在 12.Bb2 后面会跟着 12.a3！ 13.Bc1 Nxf3+ 14.Bxf3 Qf6 赢得 Nc3。

5.Bg5

1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 NG4 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.Bg5

5.Bg5 Be7 6.Bxe7（6.Bf4 Bb4+ 在 4.Bf4 变体中转置） 6...Qxe7 7.Nc3 具有危险的位置威胁 Nc3–d5。这里Borik提倡7...Qc5 8.e3 Ngxe5，此时他可以用Qc5-e7对Qd1-d5做出反应（并且d5方不再对Nc3可用），并用Nc6-e7对Nc3-d5做出反应（以交换恼人的骑士）。黑方还可以使用 7...O-O 8.Nd5 Qd8 9.e3 Ngxe5 10.Nxe5 Nxe5 延迟夺回 e5 兵。与此同时，自然7...Ngxe5落入白方的位置陷阱，在8.Nd5（“！？”Lalic）8...Qd8 9.Nxe5 Nxe5 10.Qd4 f6 11.f4 Ng6 12.Qe4+ Kf7之后，白方获得了优势。

explanations.pageTitle: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. c4/2...e6
explanations.text:
2...e6

2...e6 is a move with several purposes. First, it opens a diagonal for the development of Black's dark-squared bishop. It also challenges White's ambition in the center by attacking the d5 square. By doing so, Black prepares to play ...d5 while discouraging White from playing d5 themself.

A disadvantage for Black of systems with ...e6 is that the pawn on e6 blocks the c8-h3 diagonal on which Black's light-squared bishop may wish to operate. Finding a useful way to develop this piece, either through a queenside fianchetto or a future reopening of the c8-h3 diagonal, is a perennial challenge for Black players after ...e6. However, the inactivity of the light-squared bishop, while sometimes problematic, is rarely fatal in the early going, and should not discourage Black players from choosing 2...e6 or ...e6 on a later move.

White has three main choices here:

/3. Nc3/ - more aggressive in trying to establish a center via e2-e4, but also allows the 3...Bb4 pin (Nimzo-Indian). Black may also play a Benoni (3...c5) or QGD (3...d5).

/3. Nf3/ - Less aggressive but solid. White may face a Queen's Indian (3...b6), Benoni, Bogo-Indian (3...Bb4+), or QGD.

/3. g3/ - This usually leads to a Catalan, or sometimes a Symmetrical English or Benoni. The Catalan offers good chances for White to obtain powerful piece play in a more open game than the typical 1. d4 openings.

Less common moves include:

3. Bg5, the Seirawan attack.

3. g4, the Devin gambit.

explanations.textZh:
2...e6

2...e6 这一着棋有多种目的。首先，它为黑方黑方象的发展开辟了一条对角线。它还通过攻击d5方格来挑战白方在中路的野心。通过这样做，黑方准备下...d5，同时阻止白方自己下 d5。

黑方采用...e6 的系统的一个缺点是，e6 上的棋子阻挡了黑方的光方象可能希望操作的 c8-h3 对角线。找到一种有用的方法来发展这首曲子，无论是通过后翼前卫还是未来重新打开 c8-h3 对角线，对于 ...e6 后的黑人棋手来说是一个长期的挑战。然而，光方主教的不活动虽然有时会出现问题，但在早期很少会致命，并且不应该阻止黑方在后续行动中选择 2...e6 或 ...e6。

白棋在这里有三个主要选择：

/3。 Nc3/ - 更积极地尝试通过 e2-e4 建立中心，但也允许 3...Bb4 引脚（Nimzo-Indian）。黑棋也可以下贝诺尼 (3...c5) 或 QGD (3...d5)。

/3。 Nf3/ - 攻击性较小但坚固。白方可能面对的是 Queen's Indian (3...b6)、Benoni、Bogo-Indian (3...Bb4+) 或 QGD。

/3。 g3/ - 这通常会导致加泰罗尼亚语，有时会导致对称英语或伯诺尼语。加泰罗尼亚棋为白方提供了很好的机会，可以在比典型的 1.d4 开局更加开放的游戏中获得强大的棋子玩法。

不太常见的举动包括：

3. Bg5，Seirawan攻击。

3. g4，德文策略。

explanations.pageTitle: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3
explanations.text:
3. Nc3

With 3. Nc3, White develops a piece and continues to fight for the center of the board. On c3, the knight controls the important d5 and e4 squares. Black can choose from four main continuations.

/3...Bb4/ the Nimzo-Indian Defence, fighting for the center by pinning White's knight.

/3...d5/ transposing into the Queen's Gambit Declined.

/3...c5/ transposing into the Modern Benoni.

/3...Nc6/ transposing into a variation of the Black Knights' Tango.

/3...Nc6/ transposing into a variation of the Black Knights' Tango.
explanations.textZh:
3.NC3

有了 3. Nc3，白棋发展出一颗棋子并继续争夺棋盘的中心。在c3上，骑士控制重要的d5和e4方格。黑棋可以从四种主要的延续中进行选择。

/3...Bb4/ 尼姆佐-印度防御，通过压制白方骑士来争夺中心。

/3...d5/ 转换为后弃兵策略。

/3...c5/ 转换为现代伯诺尼。

/3...Nc6/ 转换为黑骑士探戈的变体。

explanations.pageTitle: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...Bb4
explanations.text:
3...Bb4 · Nimzo-Indian Defence

3...Bb4 introduces the Nimzo-Indian Defence. Black develops their dark-squared bishop as actively as possible and pins the white knight. If not handled properly, this pin can cause problems for White for several reasons. The most positionally significant of these is that the pin nullifies White's control of the e4 square. White would like to play e4 at some point, but Black's knight on f6 dominates the square for now, since the c3 knight cannot recapture when pinned. Consequently, Black may be able to install their knight on e4 or otherwise use the square for his own purposes if White does not fight for it.

A second implication of the pin is that Black is threatening to exchange bishop for knight and double White's pawns. The resulting position would be unbalanced, with White trying to open the position to utilize the power of his two bishops, and Black working to keep the position closed and exploit White's pawn weaknesses. White must decide how they feel about this prospect when choosing their next moves.

The Nimzo-Indian Defence is quite popular and there are a number of systems available to each side. White's fourth move options are listed below. Perhaps the most obvious move, 4. Bd2, which breaks the pin and eliminates Black's threat to double White's pawns, is not among them. 4. Bd2 does not lose immediately, but it is rarely seen in top-level chess because it is much less ambitious than White's other choices.

explanations.textZh:
3...Bb4 · 尼姆佐-印度防御

3...Bb4 介绍尼姆佐-印度防御。黑方尽可能积极地发展黑方象并钉住白马。如果处理不当，该脚可能会因多种原因给白棋带来问题。其中最重要的位置意义是该销使白方对 e4 方格的控制无效。白棋想在某个时刻下 e4，但黑棋在 f6 上的马暂时占据了方格，因为 c3 马在被压制时无法重新夺回。因此，如果白棋不为之而战，黑棋可能能够将他们的马安装在 e4 上，或者以其他方式使用该方格来达到自己的目的。

该图钉的第二个含义是黑方威胁用主教交换马和双白方的棋子。由此产生的局面将是不平衡的，白方试图打开局面以利用他的两个主教的力量，而黑方则努力保持局面封闭并利用白方棋子的弱点。白方在选择下一步行动时必须决定他们对这一前景的感受。

尼姆佐-印度防御系统非常受欢迎，双方都有许多可用的系统。下面列出了白方的第四步棋选择。也许最明显的走法 4.Bd2 并不在其中，它打破了保位并消除了黑方对白方棋子加倍的威胁。 4. Bd2不会立即失败，但在顶级国际象棋中很少见到，因为它比白棋的其他选择要小得多。

explanations.pageTitle: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...Bb4/4. a3
explanations.text:
4. a3 · Sämisch Variation

This move can be seen as the critical test of the Nimzo-Indian; White is willing to spend a tempo to force Black to carry out their plan of neutralizing the c3-knight.

With 4. a3, the Sämisch named after the German Grandmaster Friedrich Sämisch, White immediately questions the placement of the bishop. This has the benefit of seizing the bishop pair early (if Black takes the knight), and resolving central tension. White will play for an eventual e4 push after f3, often transposing to or from variations with 4. f3.

Taking the Knight is forced as the alternatives are illogical or unsafe.

4...Bxc3+ inflicts the doubled pawns on White and is the main continuation.

4...Ba5?? Maintaining the pin is an error as it just loses the bishop after 5. b4 Bb6 6. c5.

Playing 4...Be7?! is better, but it defeats the point of the Nimzo-Indian since White gets to play 5. e4 for free. (The point of the 3...Bb4 pin was to prevent White from doing this easily.)

explanations.textZh:
4. a3·萨米施变奏

此举可以被视为对尼姆佐-印度的关键考验；白棋愿意花点时间迫使黑棋执行他们压制c3骑士的计划。

对于 4. a3，以德国大师弗里德里希·萨米施 (Friedrich Sämisch) 命名的萨米施 (Sämisch)，白棋立即质疑主教的位置。这样做的好处是可以尽早夺取象对（如果黑方拿下马），并解决中心紧张局势。白棋将在 f3 之后进行最终的 e4 全推，经常与 4. f3 进行变体转换。

选择骑士是被迫的，因为其他选择不合逻辑或不安全。

4...Bxc3+ 对白方造成双兵，是主要的延续。

4...Ba5??保持 pin 是一个错误，因为它在 5. b4 Bb6 6. c5 之后失去了主教。

玩4...Be7？！更好，但它违背了 Nimzo-Indian 的要点，因为白棋可以免费下 5.e4。 （3...Bb4 针的目的是防止白棋轻易地这样做。）

explanations.text:
Sämisch Variation

5. b4

White punished black's careless play and will win black's bishop. Black may hold on to it with /5...Bb6/, but White can still play 6. c5.

萨米施变例

5.b4

白棋惩罚了黑棋的粗心行为，并赢得了黑棋的象。黑棋可能会用/5...Bb6/保住它，但白棋仍然可以下6.c5。

explanations.pageTitle: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...Bb4/4. a3/4...Bxc3
explanations.text:
4...Bxc3+

Black takes the knight with 4...Bxc3+. White must recapture with /5. bxc3/. White will have the bishop-pair and a large center, but Black will have counterplay against the weak c4-pawn.
explanations.textEn:
4...Bxc3+

explanations.textZh:
4...Bxc3+

黑方以 4...Bxc3+ 拿下马。白棋必须用/5夺回。 bxc3/.白方将拥有主教对和一个大中锋，但黑方将对弱的 c4 兵进行反击。

explanations.pageTitle: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...Bb4/4. Bg5
explanations.text:
4. Bg5 · Leningrad Variation

White decides to match Black pin for pin, and the e4 square is once more a no man's land. More subtle is the fact that Black's knight no longer controls d5 either. For that reason, van der Sterren calls the d5 advance "the point but also the necessary consequence of 4. Bg5." Either /4...h6/ 5. Bh4 c5 6. d5 or /4...c5/ 5. d5 h6 6. Bh4 is almost always played.

4. Bg5 is a fairly uncommon move against the Nimzo-Indian, being only played by 2% of Masters on the lichess opening database. With no black pawn on d5 White isn't threatening to win it like they often are against the Ragozin or Queen's Gambit Declined.

explanations.textZh:
4. Bg5·列宁格勒变奏曲

白棋决定将黑棋对垒，e4 方格再次成为无人区。更微妙的是，黑方的马也不再控制 d5。因此，范德斯特伦将 d5 的推进称为“要点，也是 4.Bg5 的必然结果”。 /4...h6/ 5. Bh4 c5 6. d5 或 /4...c5/ 5. d5 h6 6. Bh4 几乎总是被演奏。

4. Bg5 是对抗 Nimzo-Indian 的一个相当不常见的动作，在巫妖开局数据库中只有 2% 的大师使用过。由于 d5 上没有黑棋，白棋不会像他们经常对抗拉戈津或拒绝后弃兵那样威胁获胜。

explanations.pageTitle: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...Bb4/4. Bg5/4...h6
explanations.text:
Nimzo-Indian Defence, Leningrad Variation

4...h6

Black drives the bishop back, so as to gain the ability to play ...g5 and break the pin at a later time. 5. Bxf6 Bxc3 6. bxc3 Qxf6 gives up the bishop pair and lessens White's ability to defend the weak c pawns, especially once they become fixed in place with ...c5, so the only good move is 5. Bh4.
explanations.textEn:
Nimzo-Indian Defence, Leningrad Variation

4...h6

Black drives the bishop back, so as to gain the ability to play ...g5 and break the pin at a later time. 5. Bxf6 Bxc3 6. bxc3 Qxf6 gives up the bishop pair and lessens White's ability to defend the weak c pawns, especially once they become fixed in place with ...c5, so the only good move is 5. Bh4.
explanations.textZh:
尼姆佐-印度防御，列宁格勒变例

4...h6

黑方将象击退，从而获得下...g5的能力，并在稍后的时间打破销钉。 5. Bxf6 Bxc3 6. bxc3 Qxf6 放弃了象对，削弱了白方防守弱 c 兵的能力，特别是当他们用 ...c5 固定到位时，所以唯一好的走法是 5. Bh4。

explanations.pageTitle: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...Bb4/4. Bg5/4...h6/5. Bh4
explanations.text:
Nimzo-Indian Defence, Leningrad Variation

5. Bh4

The bishop retreats, since taking on f6 would accomplish nothing. Now Black has the idea of playing ...g5, but he shouldn't be too eager to weaken his kingside right away. The threat of breaking the pin is enough to keep White from playing e4 for now, so Black should address the center. 5...c5, forcing White to advance his d pawn, is the most common move, but 5...b6 is also playable, with Black either fianchettoing after 6. e3 or pushing c5 after all following 6. f3.
explanations.textEn:
Nimzo-Indian Defence, Leningrad Variation

explanations.textZh:
尼姆佐-印度防御，列宁格勒变例

5.Bh4

主教撤退了，因为对付 f6 不会有任何结果。现在黑方有下棋...g5的想法，但他不应该太急于立即削弱他的王翼。破坏旗位的威胁足以阻止白方暂时下 e4，因此黑方应该向中心进攻。 5...c5，迫使白方推进他的 d 兵，是最常见的走法，但 5...b6 也是可以下的，黑方要么在 6.e3 之后下棋，要么在 6.f3 之后推 c5。

explanations.text:
Nimzo-Indian Defence, Leningrad Variation

5...c5

Black starts to attack the center. Taking on c5 collapses White's center for no good reason, and after 6. e3 cxd4 7. exd4 d5 nothing is wrong with White's position, but it is tough to see where his advantage lies. The most common reply is therefore 6. d5, claiming space.
explanations.textEn:
Nimzo-Indian Defence, Leningrad Variation

5...c5

Black starts to attack the center. Taking on c5 collapses White's center for no good reason, and after 6. e3 cxd4 7. exd4 d5 nothing is wrong with White's position, but it is tough to see where his advantage lies. The most common reply is therefore 6. d5, claiming space.
explanations.textZh:
尼姆佐-印度防御，列宁格勒变例

5...c5

黑棋开始攻击中心。对阵c5无缘无故地瓦解了白方的中锋，在6. e3 cxd4 7. exd4 d5之后，白方的位置没有任何问题，但很难看出他的优势在哪里。因此，最常见的答复是 6.d5，要求空间。

explanations.text:
Nimzo-Indian Defence, Leningrad Variation

6. d5

White advances his center. If he can later play e4, it will be hard for Black to shake off his lack of space. Still, playing ...exd5 now and giving white a central majority would be a drastic step. Instead Black usually opts to play around White's d pawn, with ...d6 preparing ...e5, but there is another option: the so-called Averbakh Gambit. Black can sacrifice a pawn with 6...b5 7. dxe6 fxe6 8. cxb5, after which he can take the center with ...d5 and bring his rook to the half-open f file with ...O-O; the stray white pawn is usually disposed of by ...a6.

Nimzo-Indian Defence, Leningrad Variation

尼姆佐-印度防御，列宁格勒变例

6.d5

白棋推进了他的中锋。如果以后能下e4，黑方将很难摆脱空间不足的局面。尽管如此，现在玩...exd5并让白人占多数将是一个重大的一步。相反，黑方通常选择围绕白方的 d 棋子下棋，用 ...d6 准备 ...e5，但还有另一种选择：所谓的阿弗巴赫弃兵。黑方可以用 6...b5 7. dxe6 fxe6 8. cxb5 牺牲一个棋子，之后他可以用 ...d5 占据中心，并用 ...O-O 将车带到半开的 f 列；杂散的白色棋子通常由 ...a6 处理。

explanations.pageTitle: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...Bb4/4. Qc2
explanations.text:
Nimzo-Indian Defence:Classical Variation

The Classical Variation, 4.Qc2, aims to address two main problems posed by the Nimzo-Indian defence. On c2 the white queen protects the knight on c3, meaning that Black will no longer be able to double White's pawns by exchanging bishop for knight. At the same time, the queen hits the important e4 square.

A note on strategy and rules of thumb: Beginning chess players are often told not to move the queen too early in the opening. While as a general rule this advice is valuable, it is not sacrosanct. The Classical Nimzo provides an excellent opportunity to examine this rule, and its limitations, more closely. The admonition against early queen moves stems partly from the fact that the opposing player may be able to harass the queen simply by making useful developing moves. While one player is struggling to return his queen to safety, the second is gaining a decisive lead in development. In the Classical Variation, however, the queen's deployment to c2 is hardly a brazen sortie into enemy territory. It is unlikely that Black will be able to easily attack the queen anytime soon, so White's move is not considered risky.

A second reason to delay the queen's development is that the queen does not work well without the assistance of the minor pieces, and it is not clear until the knights and bishops are deployed where the queen will be most useful. With 4.Qc2, it is true that White neglects to develop a kingside piece or even to open lines for development, but it is clear that the queen will perform a useful function on c2. The fight for the e4 square is always a significant theme in Nimzo-Indian games, and the queen contributes to this fight. She also bolsters White's position on the queenside by protecting the pawn structure, and at the same time she takes aim at Black's kingside. White should not have a problem deploying the queen from c2 to whatever theater of battle requires her services.

explanations.textZh:
尼姆佐-印度防御:经典变例

经典变例 4.Qc2 旨在解决尼姆佐-印度防御带来的两个主要问题。在c2上，白后保护了c3上的马，这意味着黑方将不再能够通过将象换成马来加倍白方的棋子。与此同时，皇后击中了重要的e4格。

关于策略和经验规则的说明：国际象棋初学者经常被告知不要在开局时过早移动皇后。虽然作为一般规则，这个建议很有价值，但它并不是神圣不可侵犯的。古典尼姆佐提供了一个绝佳的机会来更仔细地研究这条规则及其局限性。对早期皇后动作的警告部分源于这样一个事实，即对方玩家可能只需做出有用的发展动作即可骚扰皇后。当一名玩家正在努力让他的女王安全返回时，第二名玩家正在取得决定性的发展领先优势。然而，在经典变例中，女王部署到 c2 并不是明目张胆地闯入敌方领土。黑棋不太可能很快就能够轻松攻击皇后，因此白棋的举动不被认为是有风险的。

延迟皇后发育的第二个原因是，如果没有小棋子的帮助，皇后就无法很好地工作，并且直到骑士和主教部署到皇后最有用的地方时才清楚。对于4.Qc2，白方确实忽略了发展王翼棋子，甚至忽略了发展的开路，但很明显，皇后将在c2上发挥有用的作用。 e4方格之争始终是尼姆佐-印度游戏中的一个重要主题，而女王在这场战斗中也做出了贡献。她还通过保护兵结构来巩固白方在后翼的位置，同时她瞄准黑方的王翼。白棋将后从c2部署到任何需要她服务的战区应该没有问题。

explanations.pageTitle: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...Bb4/4. Qc2/4...d5
explanations.text:
4…d5

The Noa variation is the third most played and second most combative way of playing the Classical/Capablanca variation in the Nimzo-Indian; second to 4…c5, the Berlin variation.

The point of the Noa variation is that, if white captures the d pawn (the most played line at master level) 5.cxd5 5…exd5 6.Bg5 6…h6 7.Bh4 and 7…g5! comes in. After the bishop retreats with 8.Bg3, the knight leaps forward with 8…Ne4!. In this position, Black has an incredibly weak kingside, but has great compensation due to the activity of the pieces and whites position being frozen up with the knight pinned to the king, and the bishop on a passive square.

Going back to the start of the variation with 4…d5, a much more solid approach for white seems to be 5.a3, essentially forcing an exchange of a bishop for a knight, however, in the ensuing lines (e.g. 5.a3 5…Bxc3 6.Qxc3 6…O-O 7.Bg5) black eventually takes the pawn with 7…dxc4 and after the queen takes, it is exposed to an incoming attack from the white bishop after black plays b6 and Ba6.

explanations.textZh:
4…d5

Noa 变奏是 Nimzo-Indian 中古典/卡帕布兰卡变奏中第三大演奏方式和第二最具战斗性的演奏方式；第二个到 4…c5，柏林变体。

Noa 变体的要点是，如果白棋吃掉了 d 棋子（大师级最常玩的线）5.cxd5 5…exd5 6.Bg5 6…h6 7.Bh4 和 7…g5！主教用 8.Bg3 撤退后，骑士用 8…Ne4! 向前跃进。在这个位置上，黑棋的王翼非常弱，但由于棋子的活动和白棋的位置被冻结，马被固定在国王上，而主教在被动的方格上，因此有很大的补偿。

回到 4…d5 变化的开始，对于白棋来说，更可靠的方法似乎是 5.a3，本质上是强制将主教交换为马，然而，在随后的行中（例如 5.a3 5…Bxc3 6.Qxc3 6…O-O 7.Bg5），黑棋最终以 7…dxc4 拿下棋子，在后棋拿下后，它就面临着传入的攻击黑棋下 b6 和 Ba6 之后，白棋主教。

explanations.pageTitle: Chess Opening Theory/1. d4/1...Nf6/2. c4/2...e6/3. Nc3/3...Bb4/4. Qc2/4...d5/5. a3/5...Bxc3/6. bxc3
explanations.text:
6. bxc3

The Pretzel Gambit (unofficial title, unrecognized in the Encyclopedia of Chess Openings) is a slightly dubious and semi-obscure gambit that allows white to play 2 different types of positional games that otherwise wouldn't occur in the main line after 6. Qxc3. while the better move after bishop takes is Qxc3, Stockfish 18 on medium depth evaluates it as completely equal (0.0 – -0.1).

6… dxc4?!

While 6…dxc4?!, taking the free pawn, looks like the best move in this position, the engine evaluates it as the 4th best move in the position, giving up whatever little advantage black had. This is because the following move for white in this position is e4! gaining central space black will not gain back, and planning to go e5 attacking the knight.

This position slightly resembles a Queen's Gambit accepted, but with a few key differences.

The gambited pawn will not be won back, as it can be defended with b5.

The c-pawn (previously the b pawn before takes) defends the d pawn and prevents the black c-pawn from advancing.

the queen supports the e4 push instead of the knight

Funnily enough, contrary to fundamental theory in the Queens Gambit accepted, the main line is to defend the weak pawn with 7... b5, because after 8. a4 (the best move for white) the only move to keep the game equal for black is 8… Bb7! applying pressure on the e-pawn, but better yet applying permanent pressure on the long diagonal. If/when white castles, they (99 times out of 100) have to castle kingside due to the weakness of the queenside, and in the future if the e-pawn ever moves, the light squared bishop will always have its sights on the king.

6… O-O

O-O is the engine favorite move (on cloud depth) of many good replies to the gambit. 7. cxd5? while not immediately losing is a very dubious and dangerous move for white. This is because: After 7... exd5, e4 is no longer a move for white and, no matter what move you play, c5! is the immediate response; the queenside is very weak and white is undeveloped.

After 6... O-O there are two simple moves the engine prefers: 7. e3, supporting the weak pawn or 7. Nf3 !? reinviting the gambit and developing a piece. If black takes the "free" pawn, they are much worse due to the fact that 8. e4! comes with a venom it didn't have earlier in the position. now white can attack with initiative.

The best move following both e3 and Nf3 is c5, a very uncanny Tarrasch type of position where white somehow has a queen on c2 and doubled pawns on c3 and c4.

after e3 and Nf3 are played (something like 6... O-O 7. e3 7... c5 8. Nf3) the computer recommends b6, and the ensuing lines are unfathomable and kafkaesque in nature, with: 8... b6 9. dxc5!? 9... Ba6!? 10. cxd5!? 10... Bxf1 11. Kxf1!? 11... Qxd5 12. cxb6! 12... axb6.

6... c5
